• oauth2-proxy's endpoints (/oauth2/start, /oauth2/callback, /oauth2/sign_out) are routed only on auth.<domain>. A host-less PathPrefix(/oauth2/) router cannot carry the tiers' TLS options, and Traefik answers 421 on it. group-gate's step-up page therefore sends the browser to https://auth.<domain>/oauth2/start?pc_method=…&rd=<app>. CI rejects router rules without Host(.
  • Keycloak's /admin and /realms/master router uses portcullis-auth-console: the same forward-auth, minus Authorization in authResponseHeaders. The admin console sends its own bearer token to the admin API; portcullis-auth would replace it with the forward-auth session's token ("You do not have permission to access this resource").

items.title: Keycloak impersonation
items.text:
Core starts Keycloak with --features-disabled=impersonation. Keycloak's own impersonation (the admin console's Impersonate button and POST /admin/realms/<realm>/users/{id}/impersonation) then answers "feature disabled", even for a Keycloak console administrator. It is off because it has none of the safeguards Portcullis needs: no fresh hardware touch, no reason, no time limit, no banner and no record the person can see. Nothing in Portcullis uses it, and core CI checks that it stays off.

Administrators sign in as someone else only through Portcullis's own start (Signing in as someone else):

  • it needs a fresh YubiKey touch by the administrator and a typed reason, and lasts at most 30 minutes;
  • the start link works once, within 2 minutes, and only in the browser that holds the administrator's own Keycloak session, so it is worthless to anyone who sees it;
  • the impersonated session carries the administrator's methods, never more: it meets a template only when the administrator's own sign-in would, and a certificate counts only when it is the administrator's;
  • it can't change anything on Portcullis's pages, reach an AI tool, add a method, confirm a fresh sign-in or complete a required action;
  • group-gate checks every request against the Hub's file impersonation.json and the token's act / pc_imp claims: an ended, unknown or overdue impersonation, a malformed claim, or a file the Hub hasn't rewritten for 5 minutes is denied at once; Keycloak logs out ended sessions within 15 seconds;
  • the headers X-Forwarded-Impersonator and X-Forwarded-Impersonation are set only by group-gate: every forward-auth middleware lists them in authResponseHeaders and the public routers strip them, so a client can't send them.

The reason is kept only in the audit, the Hub's state and file, and the Keycloak session (and on the pages that show it), never in a token, a URL or a log line.

items.title: Setup links (enroll)
items.text:
enroll-invite (enroll.<domain>/invite/*) is the only router on enroll.<domain>, without forward-auth; every other path there gets Traefik's

  1. enroll's certificate actions are only on its internal listener (enroll:8444, the invite bearer), which Traefik never routes.

  2. The token is 256 bit, stored as SHA-256, single use, bound to one LLDAP user, valid 72 h (max 7 days) and revoked by a newer link. GET only shows it (link previews must not burn it); the same-origin POST redeems it.

  3. The identity provider. enroll then acts as the hidden identity provider portcullis-invite. Keycloak shows it only for kc_idp_hint=portcullis-invite, and its first-login flow links the existing LLDAP user and never creates one. The flow uses a 10-minute HttpOnly redemption cookie scoped to /invite/, a 60 s single-use code bound to the broker redirect URI and the PKCE challenge, and an ES256 id_token.
  4. Unrouted ports. Its token / JWKS port (8445) and the Hub's invite API (8444, bearer secret; also the certificates list for the Hub's sign-in inventory, contract §9.4) are not routed by Traefik. ./portcullis invite (the CLI, through docker exec) uses a loopback-only listener (8446), the only way to invite an administrator.
  5. Admins only through the CLI. The Hub API refuses admin, portcullis-hub and every member of lldap_admin, lldap_password_manager and the core-console groups of group-gate-map.conf (LLDAP group lookup, fails closed), so a leaked API secret cannot take over an admin account. The check is repeated for API-made invites at redeem, at the authorization code and at the token exchange: a user promoted to lldap_admin after the invite was made is refused, and their pending API invites are cancelled.
  6. Passkey required. The invite session (amr inv, which meets no sign-in template: the person touches the new passkey once more to open apps) cannot finish without the passkey registration (webauthn-register-passwordless, added when the link is redeemed by enroll's service account portcullis-enroll, realm-management view-users + manage-users). enroll already held the LLDAP admin bind and Vault signing rights, so this adds no new class of power to it.
  7. Re-invites. A re-invite of a user who already has keys adds one more (spare). ./portcullis invite <user> --replace-keys (lost or stolen key) deletes the user's WebAuthn credentials and sessions first.

items.title: Service accounts and public routers
items.text:
• The Hub's LLDAP account. The Hub logs in to LLDAP as portcullis-hub (lldap_admin; LLDAP 0.6.3's lldap_password_manager cannot create users or groups). It could already start arbitrary containers through its socket proxy, so this is no new trust (contract §9.1). The account cannot sign in: Keycloak's federation filters it out ((!(uid=portcullis-hub))) and group-gate denies it (GATE_DENY_USERS).
  • Public guard. Public exceptions (the Hub's portcullis-public-<app> routers) have no forward-auth: nothing is signed in and no identity header is passed (the Hub's strip middleware deletes client copies). Their first middleware, portcullis-public-guard@docker (group-gate /public-guard), returns 403 unless the policy file (version 6) publishes the request's full hostname in public_paths, the normalised path is inside one of its patterns (prefix / exact / static files; encoded /, \, NUL or # denied, and so is any # in X-Forwarded-Uri: browsers never send fragments), and the request carries none of Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, the app's credential_headers (also in _ form), credential_cookies or credential_query. Cookie and query names are compared case-insensitively after PHP's mangling (main/php_variables.c php_register_variable_ex: leading spaces dropped, /. → _, name[...] is name, an unclosed [ → _, NUL ends the name), both raw and percent-/+-decoded; names that are not valid UTF-8 (overlong forms) are refused. It never returns identity headers. See Public exceptions.
  • Logs. The guard's logs (like group-gate's path denials) show the path with token-like segments masked as <token> and query parameter names only. Never share tokens, query values, cookies or credentials.

items.title: AI support (mcp-gate)
items.text:
Every MCP request goes through core's mcp-gate (AI support, contracts §15).

  • Token rules. The gate reads the resource from the request's host and path only (never X-Forwarded-*), accepts only Authorization: Bearer, RS256/ES256 tokens of the realm's keys (fetched from the internal Keycloak URL only, and re-fetched when the set is over 10 minutes old, so a key removed from the realm stops verifying within about 11 minutes), the exact issuer, an audience that is this resource's URL and no other URL, the resource's scope, an AI client this resource allows (never portcullis-forward-auth, portcullis-fresh-auth or an app client), an amr that meets the resource's sign-in rule (YubiKey and browser certificates never count: AI clients present none), and a username that is in the resource's population right now. An Origin header must be on the allowed list (empty by default).
  • No token passthrough. The gate never forwards the person's token, a cookie, Proxy-Authorization or any X-Forwarded-*, X-Auth-Request-*, Remote-* or X-Portcullis-* header the client sent. It sends only what the companion's identity mode defines: the person's own app credential (encrypted at rest to the gate's age key; the Hub can replace one, never read it back) or identity headers plus a caller secret. MCP tokens and browser sessions never cross: an MCP token on an app page or the people page gets a sign-in redirect or 401, and a browser session's cookies on an MCP route get 401.
  • Secrets never reach the model. No Portcullis tool takes a secret as an argument (the person types it on the Hub's own form); results never carry invite links, passwords, share tokens, provider keys or Hub secrets, and go through one redactor that fails closed. Templates mark tools that would take a secret never (Gitea's Actions secrets).
  • What companions may do. A sampling or roots request from a companion ends the tool call with an error (logged deny:sampling / deny:roots); nothing is answered to the companion. URL elicitations may point only at the app's own hosts and people.<domain>. Every companion is reachable by its alias on portcullis-proxy, so it must serve nothing without its credential or caller secret.
  • Companion names can't be taken over. The gate reaches a companion by its alias portcullis-mcp-<instance>--<companion> through Docker DNS and sends it app credentials or a caller secret. ./portcullis init, up, upgrade and restore refuse to run, and ./portcullis status fails, while any container on portcullis-proxy answers to such a name (or to a core service name) without being that companion: the alias must belong to exactly one container, listed by the instance's own compose project (portcullis-<instance>), created from the Hub's override for that instance and running the service that override gives the alias to. A Docker error fails the check closed. Residual: the check reads the labels and project membership Docker reports, which anyone with Docker access can forge (and could do far worse); apps can't, because the Hub refuses com.docker.compose.* labels in templates and custom overrides and names the projects itself.
  • The Hub's MCP listener (HUB_MCP_ADDR, :8890) is bound on all of the Hub's interfaces; every request but GET /healthz needs X-Portcullis-MCP-Secret (secrets/mcp-gate/hub-secret, compared in constant time), and no Traefik router targets the port (core CI checks it). The Hub trusts the gate's identity headers only on that listener.
  • Files. The gate files in hub_data are 0640, group 10001; at start the Hub sets every other file in its data directory that has a group or other bit to 0600 (the policy, portal and attribute files keep 0644 without write bits). The access log is 0640 in mcp_gate_data.
  • Trust networks. An identity-header companion and its app share a private internal: true network nothing else may join; the app trusts identity headers only from it. Residual: a container on the host network with NET_RAW (Docker grants it by default) can forge traffic onto that bridge from the host side. Templates with such a companion may not use host networking themselves; run other host-network apps you trust only.
  • More residuals (disconnect, app_oauth apps, the AI page) are listed in AI support → Residuals.

items.title: VPN (wg, the edge and gateways)
items.text:
The VPN adds one core service, wg, with two roles: the edge, the only PROXY v2 client of Traefik's vpnsecure, and the people role, the built-in WireGuard VPN. They share code and nothing else: each tunnel has its own WireGuard device, network stack, key, port and subnet, and there is no forwarding between stacks (the people role's only way out is the edge). Interfaces: contracts §16.

Trust chain.

  • Traefik. vpnsecure listens on portcullis-vpn-edge only (exactly Traefik and wg), trusts PROXY v2 only from wg's address there (PROXYPROTOCOL_TRUSTEDIPS = that /32), and has no forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs or insecure. A gateway's own PROXY header sent straight to vpnsecure can't arrive (gateways aren't on that network) and would never be honoured.
  • The edge. Each wired provider has one TCP port on wg's portcullis-vpn address (9001 + slot). A connection on it is admitted only when it comes from that provider's gateway address, starts with a PROXY v2 header (TCP over IPv4) within 5 s, claims a source in that provider's ranges, the provider's device list is fresh by the edge's own clock, and the source is one of its unexpired devices. Anything else is closed and counted in wg_edge_rejected_total{provider,reason} (wrong_port, wrong_gateway, no_header, slow_header, outside_ranges, stale, not_in_map, no_doc, expired for a vpn.json past its valid_until, busy). The edge then re-originates the connection to vpnsecure with a new header carrying the same address. The built-in VPN's connections are handed over in-process with their tunnel address, fixed by WireGuard's key routing.
  • Open connections are re-checked on every change of vpn.json and every 2 s, and closed when the file is gone, invalid or past its valid_until, the provider no longer owns the address or is stale, or the device is gone, expired or has another owner. They also end after 12 h (lifetime) and 1 h without traffic (idle); closes are counted in wg_edge_closed_total{provider,reason} (also revoked, pressure, and rebound when the Hub moves a provider to another slot).
  • The allowlist. VPN-only routers carry portcullis-vpnallow-<id> first: an ipAllowList of the accepted providers' ranges with no ipStrategy, so it matches the connection's address (the PROXY source), never a header. An empty set is 0.0.0.0/32 (matches nobody).
  • The binding counts only on the VPN paths. group-gate evaluates the device ↔ person binding only on /auth/vpn, /public-guard/vpn and /portal/vpn, whose middlewares sit only on vpnsecure-only routers. On its normal paths it denies every VPN-only host with the /vpn-required page before looking at the address, so a websecure request with a LAN, Docker or CGNAT address never satisfies a binding.
  • Ranges are disjoint and reserved ranges refused. No provider range may overlap another provider's, the built-in subnet, the reserved link subnet 10.214.0.0/24, the core networks, 172.16.0.0/12 or 192.168.0.0/16 (Docker's default pools, from which app networks are allocated), or under Podman 10.88.0.0/16 and 10.89.0.0/16: an address there could be a container's. The Hub refuses to wire or publish such a provider; wg and group-gate refuse a vpn.json with overlapping or reserved ranges as a backstop (every VPN request denied).

The device lists (vpn_doc). vpn.json is written by the Hub only, to the core volume vpn_doc (owned 10001:10007, setgid, 2750; the file 0640, group 10007), mounted read-write in the Hub and read-only in wg and group-gate; exactly those three are in group 10007. It holds public data only (addresses, owners, public keys), never a private key. It carries a valid_until one hour ahead and is republished every 10 minutes, so a Hub that stops publishing fails closed within the hour; a missing, unreadable or invalid file denies every VPN request. vpn_doc isn't backed up: the Hub rewrites it from its state. wg_data (10006:10001, 2750) holds only wg's status.json (0640, group 10001), which the Hub reads read-only: wg never touches the engine socket.

Edge caps. Open connections, counted from accept (connections still waiting for their PROXY header included), are capped per provider (1024), per person across all their devices and providers (128) and per client address (32); a connection over a cap is closed (busy). Above 90% of a provider's cap a new connection first closes the heaviest person's sessions on that provider that have been idle for at least 2 min (pressure); active sessions and other people's never. Filling a provider therefore takes at least 8 different people. .env sets them: PORTCULLIS_VPN_EDGE_MAX_PER_PROVIDER, _MAX_PER_USER, _MAX_PER_CLIENT, _PRESSURE_PERCENT, _PRESSURE_IDLE (wg refuses to start unless per client ≤ per person ≤ per provider).

Gateways. A wired provider's ingress service (its gateway) joins portcullis-vpn at its slot address through the Hub's override, and gets PORTCULLIS_VPN_EDGE (<wg ip>:<9001 + slot>). The Hub refuses a template whose ingress service, or any service sharing its network namespace, is a job, an AI companion, has a Traefik router or label or publishes ports; only core's pinned forwarder image (ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-forwarder, uid 65534, for clients with a real tunnel interface) may share that namespace; pid: host is refused on every service of a VPN template and network_mode: host on the ingress namespace and every routed service. Templates may never use the vpnsecure entrypoint themselves (the Hub adds it per instance) or names with the reserved portcullis-vpn prefix.

What the edge can't stop

The edge contains a buggy or misconfigured gateway: one can't claim another provider's addresses. A malicious template is outside this model, as every template source is trusted with the host: a gateway with NET_ADMIN on portcullis-vpn could spoof another gateway's address there. The doctor shows wired gateways (and services in their namespace) with NET_ADMIN, privileged or host devices (vpn_gateway_privileged). Headscale's gateway runs in userspace without them.

Keys. A client's private key never reaches the Hub, the server, a log, the audit or an AI transcript: the people page makes key pairs in the browser, and ./portcullis vpn add-device keeps the pair in shell variables and on stdin only (CI greps every logged command line). No AI tool creates a device or a configuration. The Hub's host control socket (/tmp/hub-host.sock, 0600, inside the Hub's tmpfs; never on a TCP listener) answers only the Hub's own uid, which the CLI uses through docker compose exec.

items.title: Runtime matrix
items.text: Docker (rootful) Rootless Podman core wg userspace network stack; no cap_add, no devices, no sysctls, no /dev/net/tun, not privileged; the UDP port published by the engine identical. The UDP port goes through Podman's port forwarder, which rewrites the outer source: harmless, WireGuard authenticates by key. restart: always from docker-compose.podman.yml, the key bind labelled Z by the SELinux overlay kernel or TUN WireGuard in core refused refused marketplace gateway with TUN + NET_ADMIN (NetBird, WireGuard servers) allowed; doctor vpn_gateway_privileged (Info) limited ("uses TUN/NET_ADMIN inside the rootless network namespace"): NET_ADMIN acts only in the container's own network namespace; the host needs the tun module (Rootless Podman) Headscale gateway (tailscale/tailscale, userspace) works, no capabilities works

items.title: Hub proxy secret
items.text:
The Hub has no login of its own. Every request except GET /healthz must carry X-Portcullis-Proxy-Secret equal to HUB_PROXY_SECRET (at least 32 characters, compared in constant time). Otherwise the Hub answers 403, and it refuses to start without the variable.

./portcullis init generates the secret. The core router injects it with the hub-proxy-secret@docker headers middleware, placed after portcullis-auth and portcullis-groups. So the secret is never sent to oauth2-proxy or group-gate, and only requests that passed forward-auth and the lldap_admin check carry it. A container that reaches the Hub directly on the portcullis network can't spoof X-Forwarded-User without the secret.

To rotate it, empty HUB_PROXY_SECRET in .env and run ./portcullis upgrade.

items.title: Domains service
items.text: The domains service manages added extra domains: DNS records, ACME DNS-01 for wildcard certificates, and serving those certificates to Traefik.

items.title: Network isolation
items.text:
The service sits on three networks, each with exactly the members below:

  • portcullis-domains (internal, fixed subnet 172.31.252.0/28): domains + Hub. The HTTP API (:8080) accepts connections only addressed to this subnet or loopback, never from other networks.
  • domains-egress (internet access): domains and the one-shot dns-tool. They reach ACME and the DNS providers over this, isolated from the other services.
  • portcullis-certs (internal): domains + Traefik. The certificate endpoint (:8443) uses mutual TLS with a private CA.

Traefik never routes the domains service.

items.title: API authentication
items.text:
The Hub and the domains service share a bearer secret (secrets/domains/api-secret, ≥ 32 characters, generated by ./portcullis init). Every API request (except GET /healthz) carries Authorization: Bearer <secret>, compared in constant time.

DNS credentials are sent to the service once and never appear in the Hub's state, logs, audit or errors. The service's own errors are redacted against the domain's credentials before being logged, stored or returned (providers may echo tokens or request bodies).

items.title: The dns tool
items.text:
./portcullis dns plan / setup / check (and the CAA pin after up, the relax in config apply) run the domains image's one-shot tool as the compose service dns-tool (profile tools, never started on its own). It gives the main domain's .env DNS credentials to a short-lived container only; the long-running domains service and the Hub never hold them.

  • Egress only. Its only network is domains-egress: it reaches the DNS provider and the public resolvers, nothing inside the stack. No volumes, no environment, no env_file, read-only root filesystem, uid 10004, all capabilities dropped. CI checks all of this, and that domains and dns-tool are the only members of domains-egress.
  • Credentials on stdin. ./portcullis builds one JSON object with jq, which reads each value from its own environment (env.X), so a value is never on a command line; it is piped to the tool's stdin. The credentials never appear in argv, the container's environment, docker inspect or logs. dns check sends none (the tool refuses credentials there).
  • Redaction. Every provider error is redacted against the credentials before it is printed.
  • No secrets from files. The CAA pin's account URI comes from the separate traefik-account-uri helper (Container hardening), which prints nothing else from acme.json.

secrets/domains/main-domain.env (0600) holds only Traefik's account URI (DOMAINS_MAIN_ACME_ACCOUNT_URI), for the domains service's read-only plan of the main domain. It holds no credentials.

items.title: Credentials at rest
items.text:
Everything the service stores (credentials, ACME account, per-domain state, certificates and keys) lives in one age-encrypted file (domains_data/store.age, mode 0600). The age key is secrets/domains/age.key (X25519 identity, generated by ./portcullis init), mounted read-only into domains only.

The encrypted file is in core backups (BACKUP_FILE_VOLUMES). Treat it like Vault's raft snapshot: whoever has a backup and the age key (both in secrets/) can decrypt every added domain's DNS credentials.

items.title: Certificate endpoint (domains → Traefik)
items.text:
Traefik fetches certificates from https://domains:8443/traefik/dynamic via its HTTP provider (polling every 10 s). The endpoint:

  • requires and verifies Traefik's own certificate on every interface (TLS RequireAndVerifyClientCert against a private CA)
  • returns only tls.certificates with inline PEM (cert chain + key), never routers, services, middlewares or other Traefik config
  • checks every certificate's SANs before serving: they must be exactly <d> and *.<d> for an added domain <d>, never the main domain or any host at or under it (except added subdomains of the main domain themselves)

Traefik's static config (TRAEFIK_PROVIDERS_HTTP_*) tells it to use its own certificate for this endpoint. Certificates and keys are never on a shared volume.

Private CA (generated by ./portcullis init / up):

  • CA valid 10 years, renewed < 1 year left (then all three)
  • Server certificate (DNS:domains) valid until the CA expires, renewed < 30 days left
  • Traefik's certificate valid until the CA expires, renewed < 30 days left
  • ECDSA P-256, extendedKeyUsage serverAuth / clientAuth

After any renewal, ./portcullis up / upgrade restarts domains, waits for it to be healthy, then restarts traefik, so both load the new files (neither re-reads them while running). ./portcullis status warns when a certificate expires within 30 days.

The network membership (portcullis-certs: domains + Traefik) is defense in depth; reaching the port is never enough — Traefik's certificate is required.

items.title: Public IP detection
items.text:
The service needs the server's public IPv4 and, when it has one, IPv6, to create A/AAAA records. An explicit PORTCULLIS_PUBLIC_IPV4 / _IPV6 in .env always wins (an empty _IPV6 means "no IPv6"). Otherwise ./portcullis up (and dns setup) detect them over HTTPS only (--proto =https --tlsv1.2), requiring:

  • at least two independent services to answer
  • all answers to agree
  • only global unicast addresses (no private, shared, loopback, link-local, documentation, benchmark, multicast or reserved ranges)

Anything else gives no address. Without an IPv4, the service publishes no record and sets the domain's last_error. Without an IPv6, it publishes no AAAA and removes existing AAAA records at <d> and *.<d>.

The lookups run whether or not a domain is added: the main domain's DNS check compares its A/AAAA records with these addresses too. The last detected address (secrets/domains/last-public-ipv4 / last-public-ipv6) is saved, and a failed detection keeps it (because "no IPv6" removes the AAAA records), unless the running domains service confirms that no domain is added. When ./portcullis can't tell (the service isn't running yet, as during up after a down, or doesn't answer), the last address is kept, so a transient IPv6 failure never removes the AAAA records. These two files belong to the host, not the install: ./portcullis backup leaves them out and ./portcullis restore deletes them, so a secrets/ restored on a new server never hands the old server's address to the first added domain (a failed detection there gives no address). The addresses reach the service through secrets/domains/public-ips.env (mode 0600, compose env_file), never through the compose environment:. A server that may not reach the lookup services sets PORTCULLIS_PUBLIC_IPV4 / _IPV6 in .env. With the IPv4 unknown, the service keeps the records it set before, still uses a configured IPv6 and still renews certificates.

PORTCULLIS_DOMAINS_SUBNET (the API network portcullis-domains, default 172.31.252.0/28) is validated by ./portcullis: a valid CIDR of at least /29, no overlap with the proxy or auth subnets, and equal to the existing portcullis_portcullis-domains network's subnet.

items.title: Container hardening
items.text:
• Image. Built locally from core's domains/, uid/gid 10004, no-new-privileges
  • Root filesystem. Read-write (Go runtime, lego's cache)
  • Volumes. domains_data read-write; secrets/domains/ read-only (age key, API secret group 10001, endpoint certs group 10004/0)
  • Caps. All dropped
  • Network. Three isolated networks as above
  • Limits. 512 MB memory, 1024 pids

Provider HTTP requests have a 2-minute deadline (dial, TLS, headers and body).

items.title: Hub Management
items.text:
The Hub is Portcullis's web dashboard for app templates. It lists the catalog, enables and disables apps, edits their settings and sign-in templates, and shows status and logs. It is published as ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub and run by the core docker-compose.yml (HUB_IMAGE). There is nothing to build.

Open it at https://hub.<your-domain>. It requires a Keycloak login and membership of lldap_admin.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
The Hub has six main tabs under the shared navigation (Portal · Hub · People):

  • Apps — installed apps and their instances (one per app, showing all its instances)
  • Marketplace — all available templates from every template source, with installation and template source management
  • Audit log — operation and access audit
  • Doctor — system health checks and fixes
  • Settings — global server settings (shared folders, local networks, domains)
  • People ↗ — opens the People subdomain (people.<domain>) in the same tab

items.title: Apps
items.text:
The Apps page lists every installed app (an app with at least one instance: a state entry, an enabled instance, or an operation record). The page shows:

  • Drift / missing-groups / LLDAP-sweep banners at the top (see Drift detection, Missing groups)
  • "Installed apps" heading with:
    • All backups — list of every instance's backups across all apps
    • + Add an app — opens the Marketplace
  • One app block per installed app, containing:
    • App icon, name, and "N instances" count
    • + Add instance button (for instances: multi templates) — opens the setup form
    • One instance row per instance, showing:
      • Status dot (green = all running, amber = partially running, red = stopped, gray = not started)
      • Name as <App> · <label> (or just <App> when the label equals the app name), linking to the instance page
      • First hostname (or "no web page" for router-less apps)
      • Users group name (linking to people.<domain>) and member count in parentheses, or "missing" in red when the group doesn't exist
      • Status pill: "running · n of m", "not started yet", "last \<operation> failed", or the current operation ("Enabling… show progress")
      • Enable / Disable button

For an instance with duplicate names (two instances of the same app with identical labels), the row shows its id first in muted text to distinguish them.

items.title: Marketplace
items.text:
The Marketplace page shows every template from every template source as a card, whether installed or not:

  • icon, name and one-line description
  • auth badges:
Badge Meaning SSO The app supports single sign-on via Keycloak (auth.sso) Group Access group-gate restricts the instance's hostnames to its access group (users_<app> for the default instance; auth.group_access) Group Admin The app maps the admin_<app> group to its admin role (auth.group_admin) Method forward-auth, native-oidc, header-auth, mtls, custom or public No web page The template has no host routers (e.g., a background service) Rootless: works / limited / not available Only under rootless Podman: whether the app runs there, with the reasons in its tooltip
  • tags (e.g., productivity, media)
  • footer showing:
    • For installed apps: "in use · N instances", Show in Apps (filters the Apps page to that app), and + Add instance (for multi templates)
    • For not-yet-installed apps: Install…

Below the cards, the Template sources section (moved from the old Template sources section (at the bottom of the Marketplace)) shows each configured source with its URL, update interval, and management buttons.

items.title: Setup before the first start
items.text:
Clicking Install… (Marketplace) or + Add instance (Apps, for multi templates) opens the setup form. Nothing starts until you press Start.

The form has these sections:

items.title: Name
items.text:
• Label (required, 1–64 characters): shown everywhere as <App> · <label> in the portal, Hub, My apps, and People. The Hub derives the instance id from the label as you type (lowercase, accents folded, punctuation removed, no portcullis segments, max 31 characters). For example, "Team Zürich" → nextcloud-team-zurich.
  • Instance id: editable before creation, immutable afterward. The first instance (Install…, or a single template) shows the template id with 🔒 (read-only).

items.title: Address
items.text:
• Domain picker: choose the main domain or an added extra domain (domains not yet ready are disabled)
  • Subdomain per host router: shown as [subdomain].<domain>. An empty subdomain means the added domain itself. Pre-filled from defaults; edits are kept.
  • Templates with no web page show "No web page".

items.title: Who can use it
items.text:
Only shown when the manifest declares an access_group or admin_group. Two choices:

  • New groups from the label: creates users_<id> / admin_<id> (or the manifest's group names for the first instance). For the first instance, groups with other names aren't created (only a warning) and must exist on People.
  • Existing groups: pick any existing group. The Users field excludes built-in, administrator, and permission groups; Admins may be any group.

items.title: Setup choices
items.text: The template's setup: true options with their defaults. Each shows whether it can change later in Settings or is 🔒 fixed after the first start (changing it would mean moving the data). Examples: database engine (fixed), trash retention days (changeable).

items.title: Buttons
items.text:
• Start: creates the instance, then enables it (opens the instance page and shows the progress panel; a LAN-only confirmation may appear first)
  • Save without starting: creates the instance but leaves it disabled (opens the instance page with "Created. Nothing runs yet")
  • Cancel: creates nothing

Inline errors show refused values (label, id shape, hostname collisions, unknown groups, bad setup values) under their fields. The Hub is the authority: typing a built-in group in the Users field is sent and refused inline.

LAN-only ports (file sharing and other apps)

Apps with lan_only ports (Samba port 445, Time Machine port 445, Pi-hole DNS port 53, NetBird's STUN/TURN ports) publish those ports directly on the host, bypassing Docker's network isolation and any firewall rules like ufw. Anyone on your network (or the internet, if the port is exposed through your router) can reach the port. See LAN-only ports in the hardening guide.

File-sharing apps (Samba, Time Machine) also require Local networks to be configured: an empty Local networks list keeps the app from starting (its container exits at boot, and the doctor reports local_networks_empty). Set Local networks before enabling a file-sharing app.

items.title: What happens when you enable
items.text:
Before anything starts, the Hub refuses to enable the app if:

Before anything starts, the Hub refuses to enable an instance if:

  • one of its host ports (from Settings or its custom override) overlaps a host port of another enabled instance (HTTP 409, "port 0.0.0.0:3300/tcp already claimed by enabled app …"), or
  • one of its hostnames is already used by another instance, enabled or not, or is still routed by one (HTTP 409). Every hostname has exactly one owner, because group-gate keys groups and templates by full hostname (policy v6).
  • a bound group (one chosen at setup as "Existing groups") that was a valid users group at creation is now built-in, administrator, or a permission group (HTTP 409, "can't start")

When groups mode is "new", it creates the instance's missing access and admin groups in LLDAP, as you (the enabling admin, through the same audited Users & Groups operation as creating a group): users_<id> / admin_<id> for every group the manifest declares. Existing groups are left alone. If creating a group fails, the instance isn't enabled; a group created before a later failure stays (empty — the instance needs it anyway). The progress panel's groups step lists the groups it created and the ones that already existed. When groups mode is "existing", no groups are created; the step shows "bound to \<users>, \<admins>".

The Hub then generates the instance's .env and compose override, copies the template directory to <core>/templates/<app-id>/ (shared by all instances), registers the instance's Keycloak clients (a client ID owned by another template or by nobody provable aborts the enable with HTTP 409, see Keycloak clients) and runs docker compose up. The instance is recorded as enabled only after compose up succeeds. Then the Hub publishes its group, admin paths and template to group-gate.

The Hub can't test host ports outside Docker from inside its container (a service on the host, e.g. systemd-resolved on 127.0.0.53:53), so those conflicts surface as a compose up failure. See When an operation fails.

items.title: Missing groups
items.text:
An enabled instance whose access or admin group isn't in LLDAP (deleted in LLDAP's own UI, or the instance was enabled before the Hub created groups on enable) lets nobody sign in: Keycloak and group-gate find no member. The Apps page then shows a Missing groups banner listing each such instance (by id, linking to its page) and its missing groups (checked every minute). Create missing groups creates every listed users_<id> / admin_<id> group as you (audited as group.create); Create on a row does it for one instance. Groups with other names (including bound groups) are listed with "create on the people page". Every listed group name links to its group page on people.<domain>. The new groups are empty: add the people who should have access on their pages. The Hub log's warning group … not found in keycloak points to the same button. API: GET /api/instances/missing-groups, POST /api/instances/missing-groups with {} (all) or {"ids": ["<id>"]}.

An instance's Groups tab also shows a "doesn't exist" message with a Create missing groups button when a group is gone.

items.title: Progress and Stop
items.text:
Enable, disable, restart, AI support switches, create, back up, restore and delete run in the background. Clicking the button opens a progress panel (a modal dialog) headed "Enabling Gitea" (or the operation's equivalent) and "Started by at · you can close this, it keeps going". It lists the operation's steps:

  • ✓ done, with how long the step took
  • ◐ running, with a percentage (0–100), a bar and one detail line wherever there is something to measure (e.g. per image "gitea/gitea:1.25 — 312 of 690 MB" while images download, "2 of 3" while services start)
  • ○ waiting
  • ■ stopped (at n %)
  • ↺ undone (struck through: a forward step whose effect the undo reversed)
  • ✗ failed, with the error and hint (see When an operation fails)

An enable, for example, goes through: groups (users_<id> / admin_<id>, "created" or "already exist"), the sign-in client in Keycloak, downloading images, starting services (n of m), waiting until healthy (n of m), and applying settings (start hooks, data files).

You can close the panel at any time; the operation keeps going. The instance row shows "Enabling… show progress" while it runs, and clicking that or the instance name reopens the panel. Refreshing the page, opening a second tab, or another admin opening the instance shows the same running operation with its progress. Only one operation runs per instance at a time: a second Enable (or any other operation) while one runs answers HTTP 409 with the running operation, and the UI opens its panel instead.

items.title: Stop
items.text:
Stop (with the confirmation "Stop enabling Gitea and undo what it did?") undoes what the operation did. While stopping, the panel's header reads "Stopping Gitea — undoing" and the undo steps tick off under an "Undo" separator. It ends with "Gitea was not enabled · everything is back as before" (or the operation's equivalent) and "Stopped by at ". What Stop puts back: Operation Stop does Stop unavailable Enable Containers removed; volumes this enable created removed (volumes that existed before are kept); the Keycloak client and groups deleted only if this enable created them; downloaded images kept, so a later enable resumes the download; only what this enable created is removed (pre-existing groups, clients and volumes are kept) never Disable The app turned back on never Restart The app back running as before never AI support on/off, mode The switch back as it was; AI credentials are minted again on next use never Back up The partial archive deleted; the app restarted if it was running never Restore Rolled back from the pre-restore backup never Create, restore as new The new instance removed completely never Delete The delete cancelled and the app back as before once data removal starts (the first volume): the panel shows "past the point of no return — finishing" and Stop is unavailable

Stop works at every step until the operation ends, the last one included: an app that has already started is taken down and undone. Images already downloaded are kept (they don't carry instance data), so a stopped enable followed by a new enable resumes the download where it left off.

Stop always names the operation the panel shows. If that one has ended and another admin's operation started in the meantime, the Stop is refused ("Stop refused: the operation changed — another one runs now (…), nothing was stopped"). The panel always follows its own operation to its own outcome (the Hub keeps each operation's final record by its id, the last 20 per app). When a newer operation has started since (the Hub's queued restart, a start hook that failed after an enable, another admin's operation), the panel adds a short note under its outcome, "then: Restarting (running)", with a show link that opens the newer operation; press Stop there to stop that one.

items.title: Failed undo and "Stop again"
items.text: If the undo itself fails, the panel shows the error, what is left to undo ("Not undone yet: . Stop again retries what is left"), and the Stop button changes to Stop again. Press it to retry the undo, which skips the undo steps already done. Every Stop is audited as <op>.stop (e.g. enable.stop) with the step it was pressed at.

items.title: Interrupted
items.text: If the Hub restarts while an operation runs, the panel shows it as interrupted, with Stop to clean up what it left. The note reads "interrupted: the Hub stopped while this ran. Stop undoes what it did." An interrupted restore is rolled back, and an unfinished restore as new is removed, at the next Hub start on their own (the Stop is automatic).

items.title: AI support and stop_op
items.text:
The Portcullis MCP sees the same progress (get_op, wait_for_op, both with an optional op_id that names the operation to show or wait for; list_ops for every app's current operation) and can stop an operation with stop_op. When the undo re-enables or switches something on (a disable, a delete of an enabled app, a same-instance restore, an AI switch-off), stop_op needs a confirmation that names the operation (its op_id), and the Hub refuses any other operation under that lock. A stopped enable or an AI switch that went back on are audited refused for the lifecycle action (instance.enable, ai.enable) and ok for the Stop (enable.stop, ai.stop).

API: GET /api/instances/<id>/op (?op_id=<op_id>: that operation's record), GET /api/instances/ops (every app's current operation, in short), POST /api/instances/<id>/op/stop (contract §11.7).

items.title: When an operation fails
items.text:
If enable, disable, restart or a drift action fails, the UI shows the error (in the progress panel's failed step, or a dialog for a drift action), a hint where one is known, and the last 8 KiB of docker compose's output (scrollable). Values of secret-looking variables (names containing SECRET, PASSWORD, TOKEN, KEY, …, and generated ones) from the app's and core's env are replaced with [redacted]. For address already in use / port is already allocated the hint names the port and links to the app's Settings → Host Ports: change the host port, bind it to one address, or clear it (optional ports) to disable the binding, then enable again.

A failed compose up during enable is rolled back: the Hub runs docker compose down --remove-orphans for the project (volumes are kept), so no stopped containers or network stay behind. The app stays disabled, and neither the fail-closed deny entry nor a stopped_not_enabled drift item is left over. If the rollback fails too, the error says so and the leftovers show up in Drift detection (Stop & remove).

Every operation's progress and outcome is stored per app in ${HUB_DATA_DIR}/ops/<app>.json (operation, who started it, time, steps, what it created, ok/failed, error, hint, output tail; mode 0600), and kept until the next operation on that instance. An instance row whose last operation failed shows "last enable failed" (or restart, …); its instance page shows a banner, and the Logs tab, also for an instance that is not enabled, shows the record above the container logs. The API:

GET  /api/templates/lastop/<app>   {op, op_id, at, actor, running, steps, created, ok, error?, output?, hint?, rolled_back?, …} or null

Enable, disable and restart answer 202 at once and their outcome is the op record above (fields: contract §11.7). A failed /api/drift/resolve answers with its HTTP status and a JSON body {error, op, output, hint, rolled_back}; other errors stay plain text.

items.title: Disabling an instance
items.text:
Click Disable on the instance row or its instance page. The Hub runs docker compose down for the project. The instance is marked disabled only once that succeeds. If stopping fails, the instance stays enabled and the error is shown, so you can retry instead of being left with orphaned containers. If the template is gone or its compose file is broken, the Hub falls back to docker compose -p portcullis-<id> down.

Keycloak clients are not deleted when you disable an app. Volumes are kept.

Only one operation (enable, disable, restart, backup, …) runs per app at a time. A second request while one is in progress answers HTTP 409 with the running operation, whose progress panel the UI shows (Progress and Stop).

items.title: Instance page
items.text:
Each instance has its own page (#apps/<id>, or #apps/<id>/<tab> for a specific tab). The page shows:

  • Breadcrumbs: Apps › \<App> ›
  • Header: <App> · <label> (or just <App> when the label equals the app name), status pill, Enable / Disable button
  • Operation banner (when an operation is running or failed): shows progress or error, with a Details link to the progress panel
  • Doctor line (when the doctor has findings): "Doctor: …" with a link to the Doctor tab
  • Tabs: Overview · Settings · Groups · (File sharing) · Logs · Backups · AI · (VPN) · Expert · Delete

The File sharing tab appears only for templates with person_secret credentials (Samba, Time Machine), the VPN tab only for templates with a vpn: block (Headscale).

Every instance, including the default instance, gets the same page structure. Deep links from the old #app/<id>/<tab> format redirect to #apps/<id>/<tab>.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• The Sign-in block, only for apps whose manifest declares auth.native_login (Plex): Portcullis sign-in, then the app's own login (default; the override adds portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker to every router, group = the template's access_group) or App's own login only (no Portcullis), offered only if the template allows it. Choosing the latter shows a red warning; saving writes the routers without the gateway middlewares and with public@file, publishes no group for the app, logs a warning and adds an app.sign_in entry (actor, gateway -> native) to the audit log, refusals included. See Apps with their own login.
  • The Sign-in template drop-down (see Sign-in methods and templates): Default (Standard · 2.5 / 5) or any enabled template, each with its score. Below it: the sentence of the chosen rule, how the app enforces it (per request, at sign-in, at the TLS handshake), whether browsers are asked for a YubiKey or browser certificate, and the members of the app's users and admins groups who have no method set up that meets it. Apps without a Portcullis sign-in (custom without it, public, own login only) and mtls apps show no drop-down: "This app handles its own sign-in" / "The certificate is this app's sign-in". A disabled template can't be picked (409), and a pick that would switch AI support off asks first. Saved as sign_in_template (audited settings.change, scope sign_in_template).
  • The app's options, declared by the template under settings:: one value for the instance, values per group that the Hub resolves per person, secrets, per-group records and values each person enters. See App settings.
  • Host ports declared in the manifest: rebind them, or clear optional ones to disable the binding.
  • The public exceptions block, only for apps whose manifest declares auth.public_access. See Public exceptions.

One Save sends everything you changed in the tab. The save bar says what saving does (for example "Saving restarts Immich" or "Takes effect at each person's next sign-in; no restart"). A sign-in mode or public-exception change restarts the app; a sign-in template change restarts it only when whether it asks for a certificate at sign-in changes.

Input validation:

  • A path setting is a custom path or a shared folder (picked in the setting, applied through the folder's preview: see Shared folders). A shared-folder value can't be typed or saved in the panel.
  • Path settings must be absolute host directories (not /), without : (Compose would read it as host:container) or newlines. Spaces, quotes and # are fine, because paths are quoted in the generated override.
  • Port bind addresses must be IP addresses (e.g. 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1, ::1). IPv6 is bracketed automatically.
  • No setting value may contain newlines or other control characters. Values written to the app's .env may not contain ' or \ either: they are single-quoted there.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The Overview tab shows:

  • Auth notes (how the app enforces auth, from the template)
  • Addresses: each hostname as a link, editable (see Changing hostnames below)
  • Access (VPN-only access): Reachable from the internet (default) or only Portcullis VPNs; Through every VPN provider or the live providers you tick (the built-in one is Portcullis VPN (built-in)); in server mode, for an instance with public exceptions, Public links stay on the internet (server mode). Save access asks first ("Make <id> reachable only through … ? It restarts.") and restarts the app. With no VPN wired it says "No VPN is wired yet: wire a VPN first". Saved with PUT /api/instances/{id}/reach, audited instance.reach; the AI tool is set_instance_reach (widening needs a confirmation)
  • Containers: one row per service with its name, state, and status. One-off jobs show as "setup job done" (green), "setup job failed" (red), "setup job running" (amber), or "setup job pending" (gray). Services with no container show "(none) · \<svc> · no container" in red.
  • Instance: label (editable inline), instance id, template, compose project name
  • Last operation: most recent operation (enable, restart, backup, etc.) with its status and timestamp

Editing the label: click the label to edit it inline. The change is saved with Save and updates the instance's name everywhere (portal, My apps, People, consent texts).

items.title: Groups
items.text:
The Groups tab shows the instance's access and admin groups:

  • Group name (linking to people.<domain> in a new tab)
  • Kind: "New group (manual)" for groups created at setup, or "Existing group" for bound groups, plus rule details ("rule-based: \<rule>" or "built-in LLDAP group")
  • Member count and first names of up to 3 members, with "+N" for the rest
  • Manage on People ↗ button (opens the group page in a new tab)

When a group doesn't exist, the tab shows "doesn't exist" in red with a Create missing groups button.

items.title: Logs
items.text:
The Logs tab shows:

  • The instance's last operation (with compose's output if it failed)
  • A container picker: All containers or one specific container (only the instance's services)
  • Log lines (last 100, 200, or 500 lines)
  • Refresh button to reload

items.title: Backups
items.text:
The Backups tab shows:

  • List of this instance's backups (name, size, timestamp)
  • Back up now button
  • Restore here (same-instance restore) for each backup
  • Restore as new (restore into a new instance id, with an optional label)
  • All backups button (shows backups across all instances)

See Instance backups and Restoring an instance.

items.title: AI
items.text:
The AI tab (deep link #apps/<id>/ai) shows:

  • Whether the AI can act in this instance
  • Its companions (services the AI can call)
  • The switch and mode (proactive, request-only, or off)
  • The people who can use it (based on the instance's groups)
  • A Revoke button to revoke all AI tokens for this instance
  • Recent AI activity (last N AI actions)

For AI pages (ai-chat), the tab also shows the configured model providers. Templates without AI support show the reason and, when the template names one, an alternative "not vetted by Portcullis". See AI support.

items.title: VPN
items.text:
The VPN tab (deep link #apps/<id>/vpn; templates with a vpn: block only) makes the instance a VPN provider:

  • Use for Portcullis access and, for a provider with a device hook, the refresh (15s–10m, default 60s); Save asks first. Unwiring lists the apps that accept only this provider, which become unreachable. Wiring is refused while the VPN service isn't running, or when a range overlaps the built-in subnet, a reserved range, a Docker network or another provider (PUT /api/instances/{id}/vpn-provider, audited vpn.provider_wired / vpn.provider_unwired; AI tool set_vpn_provider).
  • Ranges, devices (and how many are online), Map fresh or stale with the last refresh, the hook's last error (redacted), and a table of the devices left out with the reason.
  • Static assignments (providers with identity.source: static): an address, a person and a device name; Assign asks first ("Traffic from <ip> counts as <person>'s device <name>"), Remove per row (audited vpn.static_assigned / vpn.static_unassigned; AI tool assign_vpn_address).
  • DNS: the A records for the Portcullis hostnames, the DNS hook's error if it failed, and for dns: manual I configured them (POST /api/instances/{id}/vpn-dns/ack, audited vpn.dns_acknowledged).

items.title: Expert
items.text:
Advanced tools with direct access to the compose configuration and the containers. Compose runs with three files, later ones winning:

docker compose -p portcullis-<id> \
  -f <template>/compose.yml \
  -f ${HUB_DATA_DIR}/overrides/<id>.override.yml \
  -f ${HUB_DATA_DIR}/overrides/<id>.user.yml
  1. compose.yml (read-only). The template's file as it comes from the template source. The Hub never writes it, so source syncs always fast-forward. To change routing (subdomains, routers, middlewares), change the template in its source (see Template sources).
  2. Hub override (read-only). Generated from Settings and regenerated before every compose up: bind mounts, host ports, each router's tls.options derived from the sign-in template, router middlewares for instances with their own login, and the public-exception router with its strip middleware when on. Never hand-edited.
  3. Custom override (editable). Your own additions, stored by the Hub per instance, outside the template clone, so template syncs and updates keep it. See Custom override.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
One table with rows for every variable in the instance's .env:

Column Content Key Variable name Default What the template, the Hub, or a setting writes (shown as [set] for secrets) Source template, hub, option (from a setting), or custom (your own variable) Your value Your override (empty = using the default) Actions Override / Reset (or Remove for custom variables)

Variables you can override:

  • Any variable the template uses only in environment: blocks (map values or list items)
  • Variables you add yourself with + Add your own variable

Variables you cannot override (shown with "set by the Hub — can't be overridden"):

  • Hub-set variables: PORTCULLIS_*, COMPOSE_*, DOCKER_*, BUILDKIT_*, BUILDX_*
  • Secrets (names in the template's secret_env or secret-looking names)
  • Variables set by a setting (e.g., a port's <PORT> and <PORT>_BIND)
  • Variables the template uses outside environment: (in image tags, labels, volume sources, command, etc.)

Your overrides are written single-quoted at the end of the .env, so they win. A value may not contain ', \, line breaks, or control characters. An enabled instance restarts after each change; a disabled one gets the value at its next start.

If a template update makes one of your variables refuse (moved outside environment:, became Hub-set, or became a secret), it is no longer written and shows in the Deliveries panel's "Environment values" unit. The next prune removes it.

items.title: Other Expert tools
items.text:
• Container shell: Runs one command with /bin/sh -c in a chosen container through the Engine API and shows its output. The Hub stops waiting after 15 minutes, or when the browser request is cancelled. A process that keeps running inside the container is not killed.
  • Restart app (enabled instances): A full down + up of the project, so override and env changes take effect. It waits for the result and, if it fails, shows compose's output like a failed enable.

items.title: Delete
items.text:
The Delete tab shows:

  • A warning about what will be deleted (volumes, groups, Keycloak clients)
  • For bound instances (groups mode "existing"), a note that the groups won't be deleted
  • A typed confirmation field (type the instance id to confirm)
  • Delete button

See Deleting an instance.

items.title: Custom override
items.text:
Typical uses: pin a different image tag, add environment variables, resource limits, extra bind mounts or named volumes, extra (literal) host ports, a healthcheck. Save override validates and stores it; it applies on the next restart ("restart to apply"), or when a disabled app is enabled. Saving an empty (or comment-only) override deletes the file. Every save, removal and refusal goes to the audit log as app.compose_override with the signed-in user, the size and a SHA-256 prefix, never the content (it may hold env values). The file is mode 0600.

The Hub refuses anything that would bypass Portcullis' routing or isolation. group-gate keys every policy and group by the full hostnames of the instance's Traefik routers (policy v6), and the Hub's override sets each router's TLS options and middlewares, so the custom override may not change them:

  • Top level: only services, volumes, networks. Must be a mapping; no YAML tags (compose's !reset / !override could strip the template's labels or networks).
  • Services: only services the template defines, and only these keys: image, command, entrypoint, environment, labels, volumes, ports, expose, restart, healthcheck, user, working_dir, hostname, domainname, mem_limit, mem_reservation, memswap_limit, mem_swappiness, cpus, cpu_shares, cpuset, pids_limit, shm_size, ulimits, logging, tmpfs, extra_hosts, dns, dns_search, dns_opt, stop_grace_period, stop_signal, init, read_only, cap_drop, tty, stdin_open, pull_policy, platform, depends_on (on the template's services), oom_score_adj. Everything else is refused, in particular privileged, cap_add, devices, security_opt, network_mode, networks, pid, ipc, uts, userns_mode, cgroup, cgroup_parent, sysctls, volumes_from, extends, env_file, build, links, external_links, container_name, profiles, deploy, configs, secrets, group_add, runtime.
  • Labels: no traefik.* (routers, rules, middlewares, TLS options, entrypoints, services) and no com.docker.compose.* (the Hub finds the app's containers by them).

  • Volumes: named volumes, ./templates/<app>/…, or bind mounts of absolute host paths under the bind roots; everything else is refused, including /home, /var, /opt and /etc/localtime. The bind roots are HUB_OVERRIDE_BIND_ROOTS (colon-separated absolute paths, e.g. /srv:/mnt/media), default /srv:/mnt:/media. The Hub refuses to start if a root is /, is or contains a system path (/etc, /var/lib, /run, /usr, /tmp, …), contains the Docker socket or state, or overlaps the core checkout. Sources are cleaned (//, /./); .. segments, sockets (*.sock) and / itself are refused, as are shared/slave bind propagation and volume types other than bind, volume, tmpfs.

    Warning

    The Hub can't resolve symlinks on the host: a symlink under a bind root pointing elsewhere (e.g. /srv/x -> /) would be followed by the Docker daemon. What lives under the bind roots is the operator's responsibility; keep them to data directories.

  • Ports: literal host ports only (no variables); they count in the port checks against other enabled apps and against the app's own Settings ports.

  • Top-level volumes: only labels per volume (no driver, driver_opts, external or name: they could point at host paths or another app's data).
  • Top-level networks: only networks the template declares and doesn't mark external or name (so never portcullis-proxy), with labels, driver_opts, enable_ipv6, ipam.
  • No variables anywhere. Compose interpolates ${VAR} / $VAR in keys and values after the Hub's checks, so a label key ${T}raefik.enable would become traefik.enable. Every key and value with an unescaped $ is refused; write $$ for a literal dollar sign (compose turns it into $).

Because of these rules, the routes, subdomains, published snapshot and exposure drift the Hub computes from the template stay exact with a custom override in place. The override is checked again before every compose up: if a template update dropped a service it names (or it no longer passes), enable, restart and drift actions fail with HTTP 409 ("the custom compose override (Expert) is not valid for this template any more") before compose runs — edit or clear it.

Warning

A custom override can still break the app (a wrong image, a bad mount). It can't change how Portcullis routes and guards it.

items.title: Public exceptions
items.text:
Some apps have share links meant for people without a Portcullis account (Nextcloud public shares, Grafana shared dashboards, Immich shared links). If the template declares them, the Settings tab shows a Public exceptions block (bordered in amber):

  • the template's description and every declared path with its description and kind: per share ({token} path), supporting, always opened (static assets) or all shares only;
  • a red warning: requests to these paths skip Portcullis entirely (no forward-auth, no group-gate, no hardware key); only the app's own checks (share token, share password, expiry) apply;
  • what is refused or stripped: core's public guard answers 403 to requests carrying Authorization, Proxy-Authorization or the app's login headers, cookies or query parameters (an app user signed in with "remember me" opens shares in a private window), and the Hub strips identity headers;
  • if the app's template requires a YubiKey or browser certificate at the TLS handshake (protected@file or protected-any@file), an amber warning that all of the app's routers use authaware@file while a public path is open. For native-OIDC apps it adds that the certificate is then only enforced at sign-in (Keycloak's template check); for forward-auth / header-auth apps that group-gate still checks the certificate on every gated request; and it lists routers without group-gate, which lose the handshake check. See Sign-in methods → Public exceptions.

Controls:

Control Meaning Allow public exceptions On/off (an explicit admin choice) Use the template default Forget the choice; the template's enabled_by_default applies, also after it changes on a template sync Only listed shares / All shares Mode, if the template has {token} paths. Only listed: just the shares below. All: every share of the app Listed shares Each listed token with Remove; a text box takes share URLs or bare tokens, one per line

The Hub extracts the token from a pasted URL (the {token} segment of the first matching path, e.g. https://cloud.example.org/s/AbC123/download → AbC123), checks it against the template's token_pattern and the alphabet [A-Za-z0-9._~-], rejects anything else (the save fails with the reason), and removes duplicates. At most 200 shares per app (each adds two matchers per {token} path to one Traefik rule). The status line shows what is open (with {token}, never the tokens) and on which subdomains, or "No public router is generated" — the case in mode listed with no share, which also keeps the handshake tier.

The list is admin-managed: ordinary app users can't publish a share to the internet themselves; they create the share in the app as usual (with its own password and expiry) and ask a Hub admin to list it. Remove the token (or turn the exception off) to close it again; the app's own share settings keep applying either way.

Saving regenerates the override and restarts the app. Any public choice (toggle, token list) also pins the mode it was made under, so a later template change can't widen it. Fail closed:

  • a stored mode the template no longer supports (e.g. listed after the template dropped its {token} paths) opens nothing and shows "public exception disabled … confirm a mode" in the block and as drift;
  • listed tokens the template's token_pattern no longer accepts are not routed and are shown as invalid (saving removes them).

The router is generated from the manifest, not shipped in compose.yml: only the Hub knows whether the exception is on, which shares are listed and which TLS tier the host gets, and a template can't open paths by itself.

items.title: App settings
items.text:
Templates declare their options under settings: in the manifest (Manifest Reference, contracts §13). The Hub validates every value, stores it, works out who gets what and delivers it to the app. The template only says what the option is and how the app reads it.

The panel is the app's (or instance's) Settings tab on hub.<domain>, for admins only. It needs Users & Groups: per-person values are worked out from group memberships, so without the Hub's LLDAP account the settings API answers 503 and the tab can't load. A request without a signed-in user is 401, and delegates get 403.

items.title: What the panel shows
items.text:
From top to bottom:

  1. The Deliveries strip: how each part of the last delivery went, with Retry (see Deliveries and Retry).
  2. The template's options, grouped by the template's sections. Each option shows its label, when a change takes effect ("applies: at the next sign-in", "applies: after a restart", …), its description and any warnings.
  3. Host ports, the sign-in block, the sign-in template and public exceptions (see Settings).
  4. The save bar.

Each option is one of four kinds, depending on its scope:

Scope What you set Example instance One value for the whole instance Immich's trash days, Jellyfin's library folders, Nextcloud's default quota per person A value for "everyone else with access" plus rows for groups; the Hub resolves one value per person Immich's storage quota and role, Grafana's role per group One record per group you add; the app gets the records, the Hub doesn't resolve them per person A library or room per group entered by each person Nothing: each person enters their own value on My apps Firefox Sync's Mozilla account ID

The editor fits the option's type: a text box (with the template's pattern or format), a number with its unit, a size (a number plus MiB / GiB / TiB, with an unlimited box where the template allows it), a duration, a checkbox, a dropdown, a multi-select, a list, a table, a group or user picker, or a host path (with "the app writes here as uid:gid" when the template says which identity the app writes as). Options the template pairs with requires (a Craft app's version and its SHA-256) sit side by side: setting one without the other is refused. Leaving an instance option empty (or resetting it) goes back to the template's default.

items.title: Per-group values
items.text:
A per-person option has a row Everyone else with access (the default) and one row per group. + Add group adds a row; ✕ removes it. The When someone is in several groups choice says how the Hub picks one value for a person who is in several of the listed groups:

Choice Rule largest wins / smallest wins Numbers, sizes, durations and choices (by the template's order); unlimited beats any number under "largest" and loses under "smallest" first matching group wins (in this order) Any type. The rows get drag handles and ▲ / ▼ buttons to order them everything any of their groups gives / only what all of their groups give Lists and sets on if any of their groups says on / on only if all of their groups say on Checkboxes

The template sets the rule; it may let you switch between a few (its resolve_choices). The default row is only a fallback: it applies to people in none of the listed groups and never takes part in "largest wins". If nothing applies to someone (no matching row, no default), they get nothing for that option and the app uses its own default ("unresolved: the app's own default applies").

A template can preset rows for the instance's own groups: Immich and Grafana give their admin group (admin_<id>) the administrator role. These rows are added when the instance is created or enabled, and bound to the group the Hub creates for it.

Rows follow the group, not its name. Each row stores the group's LLDAP id. When a group is deleted, through the Hub or in LLDAP's own UI, its rows stop granting anything at once and are removed (see Groups deleted outside the Hub). A group re-created with the same name starts with no rows. If you saved from a panel that was loaded before such a change, the save is refused with 409 ("re-created since its row was saved"): reload the tab.

Privileged options. Options the template marks privileged (a role or an admin flag) take rows only from groups that delegates can't steer: manual groups, and rule-based groups whose rules use admin-only fields. The group picker greys out the other groups with the reason ("can't grant a privileged value: its rule uses fields delegates can edit: office_location"). Their default is always the lowest value (Viewer, User). A group used in a privileged row becomes a guarding group.

items.title: Who gets what
items.text:
Under each per-person option, Who gets what lists everyone with access and the value they would get with the panel as it is now, before you save: "10 GiB from office_milan", "2 TiB largest of office_milan (10 GiB), it_staff (2 TiB)", "500 GiB everyone else with access". It updates a moment after each edit, has a search box and shows 50 people per page. Each group it names links to the group's page on people.<domain>, in a new tab (an unsaved draft stays where it is). The save bar adds "Changes: N people get a new value".

"With access" means:

  • with group access on (or the app's Keycloak access role enforced): the members of the instance's access group, minus anyone whose temporary membership has expired;
  • otherwise every LLDAP user except the Hub's service account.

The admin group never adds anyone: a member of admin_<id> who isn't in the access group can't reach the app and gets nothing. Warnings below the list say when some members of a listed group have no access ("1 member of office_milan has no access to Immich and gets nothing") and when people joining or leaving restarts the app. For an app signed in with its own login only (no Portcullis), nobody gets a per-person value: "per-person values need Portcullis sign-in".

items.title: Saving and when changes take effect
items.text:
The save bar says what saving does before you click Save. Each option declares when a change takes effect:

Applies What happens at once (live) A hook in the running app applies it; no restart after a reload (reload) The Hub sends the app's reload signal (or runs its reload hook) at the next request (next_request) Request headers: each person's next request carries the new value at the next sign-in (next_sign_in) Token claims: each person gets the new value when they next sign in to the app after a restart (restart) The Hub restarts the app in the background when an account is created (account_creation) Only accounts the app creates from now on get it. The panel warns "existing accounts keep their value"

One save does the strongest thing any changed option needs, once: a restart covers a reload, and several reloads are one. Changing a port, a path or an option the app reads from its .env restarts an enabled app. On a disabled app the values are stored and used at the next start.

  • A save never waits for a running delivery. If one is still running (a slow hook, a restart), the save is stored and answers at once; its delivery runs right after (the save's answer shows the Delivery unit as busy: "a delivery is running: this one follows it").
  • A restart owed survives a Hub restart. The Hub records the reload or restart a save still owes before it starts it, and runs it again at its next start if it stopped first. A restart that can't start (another operation holds the app too long) is the app's last operation restart, failed; it stays owed.
  • A restart checks before it stops the app. The Hub writes the override, .env and data files first; if one of them is refused, the app keeps running and the restart fails.
  • One bad value never blocks the .env. A stored value that can't be written into the .env (it holds a ', a \ or a line break, e.g. after a template update) is written empty for that variable only, logged, and shown in the Deliveries strip as unit env:values; every other variable is written.

Membership changes deliver too. When people join or leave a group, the Hub waits 60 seconds per instance before delivering, so many changes in a row cause one restart, not one each. It also re-checks every 10 minutes.

Every changed option is audited as settings.change (scope=…: before -> after; secrets show as replaced), refused saves as refused.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
Options of type secret (an API key, a password the app needs) are write-only. The panel shows Set ✓ (updated …) or "not set", with Replace, Generate (when the template declares how) and Clear (asks first). The input is a password field. After a save the panel is rebuilt from the Hub, which never sends a secret back: not in the panel, not in the save's answer, not in logs, op records or the audit (which says replaced, generated or cleared). Generated values use the template's length and character set (hex, letters and digits, or printable ASCII without space, ' and \). A secret can't contain ' or control characters. Clearing a secret another option requires is refused.

The Hub keeps secrets in ${HUB_DATA_DIR}/settings/<id>/secrets.json (mode 0600). They reach the app only through its .env (mode 0600), a secrets file (mode 0600, see Security & Hardening) or a hook's standard input. Expert → Environment variables shows them as [set] and refuses to override a variable an option owns ("change it under Settings") or a secret ("use Settings"). Backups carry them; a restore into a new id generates new values for the generated ones.

A template update that renames or removes a secret option doesn't leave the value behind: the next sync blanks every .env variable that still holds it before the Hub forgets it, and Expert → Environment variables shows any variable whose value equals a stored secret as [set], whoever wrote it.

items.title: Deliveries and Retry
items.text:
The Deliveries strip lists each part of the last delivery:

Unit What it is Environment The option values in the app's .env, read when the app starts Environment values (env:values) Shown only while some stored value can't go in the .env: those variables are written empty (named, without the value), and env overrides the template now refuses are skipped Data file <name> A JSON file the Hub writes for the app (mounted read-only) Hook <name> A command the Hub ran in the app's container, with the settings on its standard input Sign-in claim <attribute> Per-person values in Keycloak tokens Request headers Per-person X-Forwarded-Attr-* headers group-gate adds Reload / Restart The effect of the save Delivery The run as a whole (shown when it didn't run)

Each one reads last applied, failed: with the error (secrets blanked), or a skip reason:

Skip reason Meaning unchanged Nothing new to deliver not running The app isn't running; it gets the values when it starts directory unavailable Users & Groups didn't answer; the last delivery stays in place busy Another operation on the app was running; the delivery runs again shortly superseded A newer save replaced this run, which runs again not supported The app has no reload action previous run still running A hook from an earlier run is still running (it timed out but the container hasn't finished it); the Hub tries again

Retry runs the delivery again, every hook included, and is audited as settings.retry. A failed hook or reload is also the app's last operation, and every failed unit is logged by the Hub (settings: <id>: delivery unit <unit> failed: …). A hook runs again on its next trigger anyway, so fix the cause, then Retry.

Hooks run one at a time per instance, each for at most its template's timeout (at most 10 minutes). Nextcloud's start hook waits for Nextcloud to finish installing, which can take up to 10 minutes on the first start; a save made meanwhile is delivered after it.

items.title: Values people enter
items.text:
An option entered by each person shows, instead of an editor:

  • "N of M people with access have entered one", with a search box;
  • each value with the person, when and by whom it was set, and delivered;
  • Stored, not delivered: values the app doesn't get, with the reason: no access (the person left the access group), account changed (the account was deleted or re-created outside the Hub) or directory unavailable;
  • Not set: people with access who haven't entered one.

Clear works on every value. Set / Edit appear only when the template allows admins to enter a value for someone (admin_override), and never on a "no access" or "directory unavailable" row. These buttons act at once (they don't go through the save bar, and your unsaved edits are kept). Uniqueness applies to admins too. If the app restarts to pick values up, the option warns "people entering or changing a value restarts ".

What happens to a value:

  • Leaving the access group: the value is kept but no longer delivered. Rejoining delivers it again.
  • Account deleted through the Hub: the person's values are deleted in every app (audited, the admin as actor).
  • Account deleted or re-created outside the Hub: each value remembers the LLDAP account it was entered for. A re-created account with the same name doesn't get it; the value stops being delivered at once and is removed at the next check (audited, actor hub), only while LLDAP looks healthy (the same check as the stale-record cleanup).
  • Disabled app: values are kept, nothing is delivered.
  • Template update that removes the option, changes its type or tightens its rules: values that no longer fit are dropped (audited invalidated). When an option becomes unique, the earliest of two equal values stays.
  • Backups carry the values; a restore keeps the account check.

Every change, refusal, deletion and purge is audited as settings.person_value with target <instance>/<option>/<person>.

items.title: App instances
items.text:
A template can run as multiple fully independent instances. Each instance has its own:

  • compose project, containers and volumes (data is never shared)
  • label (shown as <App> · <label> everywhere)
  • settings, environment variables and generated secrets
  • Keycloak clients (one per manifest keycloak_clients entry)
  • access and admin groups (users_<id>, admin_<id>, or bound existing groups)
  • sign-in template pick, public exceptions and sign-in mode
  • drift tracking and last-operation record

Templates declare instances: multi or instances: single in their manifest. Multi templates show + Add instance in Apps and Marketplace and can be instantiated as many times as needed. Single templates run only as their default instance (e.g., templates that bind fixed hardware).
