A token with amr=mtls or amr=file proves that a certificate was used at login. group-gate counts a certificate method only while the current request carries a certificate of that kind that is not revoked and whose CN equals the session's preferred_username. It tells the kinds apart by the certificate's issuer, compared with the two CA files it mounts (certs/yubikey-ca.crt and certs/browser-ca.crt); if the two CAs had the same name, or either file can't be read, no certificate counts. A template that needs the certificate then shows the present-certificate page, the step-up page or the needs-stronger page.

So a session opened with a certificate that is revoked later stops working normally within a minute. So does a session replayed from another browser without it.

items.title: Revocation
items.text:
./portcullis cert list                # find the serial and its KIND (--all includes revoked)
./portcullis cert revoke <serial>     # revoke (add --yes to skip the prompt)
./portcullis cert sync                # rewrite the serial list from Vault

People revoke their own browser certificates on the Sign-in page; admins and sign-in helpers revoke anyone's (but an administrator's) on the person's Sign-in tab. A revoked certificate normally stops working within a minute and shows as revoked everywhere (the Sign-in page, the Sign-in tab, cert list --all).

Traefik does not check CRLs. A TLS handshake with a revoked but unexpired certificate still succeeds. Revocation is enforced in three places:

  1. group-gate, on every request (portcullis-groups@docker). client-headers@file or client-cert-pem@file (Traefik passTLSClientCert with serialNumber: true) passes X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info to the backend and to every later forward-auth middleware. group-gate returns 403 when the certificate's serial is revoked, before any other check. It has two sources:
    • The serial list certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt. cert revoke and cert sync rewrite it atomically from Vault's lists of revoked serials of both CAs, and group-gate re-reads it when it changes. If Vault can't be queried, the file is left unchanged and the command fails: it never "un-revokes" by writing an empty list. If the file exists but can't be read, group-gate denies every request that presents a certificate (fail closed).
    • Vault's full and delta CRLs of both CAs (GATE_CRL_URLS = http://vault:8200/v1/pki_int/crl http://vault:8200/v1/pki_file/crl, GATE_DELTA_CRL_URLS = the two .../crl/delta), re-fetched every 60 s (GATE_CRL_REFRESH_SECONDS). The union is enforced. A revocation on the web or with cert revoke rotates its CA's full CRL at once, so it is enforced within 60 s. Revocations made directly through the Vault API or UI reach the delta CRL within about 2 minutes (Vault's periodic rebuild runs once a minute) and are denied at group-gate's next refresh. If Vault is unreachable, the last good copy of each CRL is kept and the serial list still applies.
  2. Keycloak certificate login: each certificate step checks its own CA's CRLs (above). It fails closed when the CRL is unavailable or stale.
  3. Certificate binding: sessions on templates that need a certificate need the unrevoked certificate on every request.

Coverage. Revocation covers:

  • every router whose middleware chain has client-headers@file or client-cert-pem@file before portcullis-groups@docker (all core routers and the default templates)
  • new Keycloak certificate logins
  • sessions on templates that need a certificate

Not covered. Routers that rely on the TLS handshake alone, e.g. a protected-tier router without portcullis-groups@docker. There the certificate works until it expires. Password and passkey sessions of the same user are also not affected; sign them out in the Keycloak admin console if needed.

items.title: Internal certificate authority
items.text:
Vault holds the internal certificate authority: a root (pki) and two intermediates signed by it, one per certificate kind:

Mount CN Issues Role Exported as pki <domain> Root CA the two intermediates — certs/root-ca.crt pki_int <domain> Intermediate CA (the YubiKey CA) YubiKey certificates client-cert certs/yubikey-ca.crt (also certs/intermediate-ca.crt) pki_file <domain> Browser Certificate CA browser certificates browser-cert certs/browser-ca.crt

./portcullis pki setup creates them and keeps them in place:

  • pki_file has a 43800 h (5-year) lifetime and the same URL and CRL configuration as pki_int (expiry=72h auto_rebuild=true auto_rebuild_grace_period=12h enable_delta=true delta_rebuild_interval=1m).
  • The browser-cert role copies the client-cert role's settings (client certificates only, EC P-256 keys, the CN never taken from a request, max_ttl=$CLIENT_CERT_TTL) and is rewritten on every run.
  • certs/ca-chain.crt is root + pki_int + pki_file, in that order (the protected-any and authaware TLS options), certs/ca-chain-yubikey.crt is pki_int alone, without the root (the protected option, so a browser certificate never passes it: Traefik trusts every certificate in that file as an anchor and uses the intermediates the browser sends, and a browser certificate's .p12 carries pki_file and the root), and Keycloak's truststore (certs/truststore/) gets portcullis-ca-chain.pem, portcullis-yubikey-ca.pem and portcullis-browser-ca.pem. Whenever pki_file is created or either chain on disk is out of date, pki setup rewrites both chain files and the truststore, and the next ./portcullis up restarts Traefik and Keycloak so they load them.
  • It refuses (exit 1) when the two intermediates would have the same CN: every reader tells the kinds apart by issuer.
  • It creates pki_file when it is missing, even while pki_int exists.
  • --force destroys both CAs.

items.title: Vault: server mode, auto-unseal and AppRole
items.text:
Vault runs in server mode with integrated (raft) storage on the vault_data volume (vault/vault.hcl, data in /vault/file), so the CA survives restarts. The listener is plain HTTP on the internal portcullis network, and on 127.0.0.1:8200 on the host only. The container runs as the image's non-root vault user (100:1000).

./portcullis vault init is idempotent and is run by init, upgrade and restore. It does three things:

  1. Init, on the first run only, with one key share, threshold 1. It writes to secrets/ (dir 0700, gitignored):
    • secrets/vault-init.json: the root token and unseal key (0600)
    • secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key: mounted read-only into the vault container. Owned by you, group 1000, 0640 (dir 0750)
  2. Unseal. After that, vault/entrypoint.sh unseals automatically on every container start: up, restart, host reboot.
  3. Least privilege for enroll. It creates the AppRole portcullis-enroll with policy vault/policies/enroll.hcl, which allows only signing (pki_int/sign/client-cert, pki_file/sign/browser-cert), listing (pki_int/certs, pki_file/certs) and reading (pki_int/cert/*, pki_file/cert/*) certificates, revoking (pki_int/revoke, pki_file/revoke) and rotating the CRLs (pki_int/crl/rotate, pki_file/crl/rotate). The credentials in secrets/enroll/ (group 10002 = the enroll user, 0640) are mounted read-only into enroll. Enroll logs in for 1-hour tokens and logs in again before expiry or on a 403. There is no static or root token in .env. Rotate the secret-id with ./portcullis vault rotate-enroll-secret.

The admin commands (pki setup, cert enroll|renew|revoke|list|sync, status) use the root token from secrets/vault-init.json, or VAULT_TOKEN if exported. They use the host vault CLI if it is installed, otherwise the CLI inside the vault container. The token is passed by environment-variable name, never on the command line. secrets/ and backups/ are masked from the Hub container with empty tmpfs mounts.

pki setup is idempotent and never replaces an existing CA: it only recreates missing pieces such as pki_file, the client-cert and browser-cert roles or the exported CA files. If it finds an incomplete PKI (an earlier run aborted before the intermediate was signed), it wipes and recreates it; any Vault error aborts instead of being mistaken for "no PKI". If Vault has no CA but certs/ca-chain.crt exists (Vault data lost), it refuses to create a new one. Restore a backup, or pass --force and issue every certificate again. See the CLI Reference.

certs/server.key is written 0640 with group 0 (Traefik runs as root but without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE). When the CLI is not run as root, it changes group ownership through a throwaway root container (pinned alpine, only CAP_CHOWN, no network).

Trade-off of auto-unseal. The unseal key lives on the same host as the encrypted data. Root on the host, or anyone who can read secrets/, can unseal Vault. What it does protect: a copy of the vault_data volume alone is useless. Several Shamir shares on the same disk would add nothing, hence one share.

For stronger guarantees, remove the secrets/vault-unseal mount and unseal by hand after each restart (docker compose exec vault vault operator unseal), or use a cloud KMS auto-unseal.

Keep an offline copy of secrets/vault-init.json. Backups made by portcullis backup and upgrade include secrets/ (and a raft snapshot of Vault), so protect them like the keys themselves. Off-host copies are encrypted with BACKUP_PASSWORD (see Backups).

items.title: Without YubiKey or browser certificates
items.text:
Switch the YubiKey certificate method off (and leave Browser certificate off) in Hub → Settings → Sign-in (once no enabled template needs them: Standard, for instance, still accepts any passkey). Then no app asks for a certificate any more: every app whose template has no certificate method left gets the public tier, and sign-in is passkeys only (plus passwords, if you switch them on). Core pages keep the optional certificate request; a browser without a certificate shows nothing. You don't need ykman or PIV setup.

mtls apps rely on the certificate alone

An app with auth.method: mtls has no forward-auth: the YubiKey certificate at the TLS handshake is its sign-in, and it always keeps the protected tier, which trusts only the YubiKey certificate authority (a browser certificate is refused at the handshake). Without issued YubiKey certificates nobody reaches it.

items.title: Common scenarios
items.text: Scenario ACME_STAGING YubiKey certificate method Notes First DNS/ACME experiments true off Untrusted certs, passkeys only Production, passkeys only false off Trusted certs, no certificate management Production, with YubiKey certificates false on PIV certificates for browsers and CLI/API, passkeys too; browser certificates optional Development / CI true on Everything, including certificate flows

items.title: "Your connection is not private" / NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID
items.text: You are on staging certificates. Switch to ACME_STAGING=false, or launch Chrome with --ignore-certificate-errors.

items.title: App shows "unable to get local issuer certificate"
items.text:
The app container cannot verify Keycloak's TLS cert. Check that:

  • certs/ca-bundle.crt exists (./portcullis config apply --bundle-only)
  • the container mounts it (./certs/ca-bundle.crt:<path>:ro in the template's compose.yml)
  • the runtime uses it: NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for Node.js, SSL_CERT_FILE for Go

items.title: ERR_BAD_SSL_CLIENT_AUTH_CERT
items.text: The YubiKey or browser certificate is invalid, expired, or not issued by the internal certificate authority. Renew a YubiKey certificate on the Sign-in page while it is still valid (otherwise an admin issues a new one); create a new browser certificate there.

items.title: ERR_SSL_CLIENT_AUTH_CERT_NEEDED
items.text: The router is on the protected tier (a YubiKey certificate required; a browser certificate is never accepted there) or protected-any (a YubiKey or browser certificate required). Get a YubiKey certificate (or, on protected-any, create a browser certificate), or move the app to a template that doesn't need a certificate in every alternative (Hub → the app's Settings).

items.title: 403: the certificate has been revoked
items.text: group-gate found the certificate's serial in the revoked list or a CRL. Remove it from the browser/keychain; then create a new browser certificate on the Sign-in page, or have an admin issue a new YubiKey certificate.

items.title: 403: the certificate revocation list is unavailable
items.text: group-gate cannot read certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt and therefore denies requests that present a cert. Run ./portcullis cert sync and check the file's permissions.

items.title: Certificate login in Keycloak does nothing
items.text:
Check the Keycloak logs:

  • HTTP header "X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert" is not trusted means the request did not come from Traefik's portcullis-auth address. Check PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP and that Traefik is attached to portcullis-auth.
  • A CRL error means Vault is sealed or unreachable (./portcullis status).
  • portcullis ERROR naming a CA file: certs/truststore/portcullis-yubikey-ca.pem or portcullis-browser-ca.pem is missing or not a CA. Run ./portcullis pki setup && ./portcullis up.
  • No certificate attempt at all: that certificate's method is off (Settings → Sign-in), or Keycloak has no valid signin-keycloak.json from the Hub (every method off, see Sign-in flows in Keycloak).

items.title: DNS Configuration
items.text: Portcullis uses wildcard DNS to route all subdomains to a single server. This page covers the records Portcullis wants (its DNS plan), how ./portcullis dns plan / setup / check creates and checks them, CAA and DNSSEC, and the DNS provider credentials for automatic certificate issuance.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A domain you control (e.g., example.com)
  • DNS hosted on a supported provider (Cloudflare, Porkbun, Route 53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner (legacy DNS or Hetzner Cloud), or any lego provider, whose records you then create by hand)
  • A server with a public IP running Portcullis

items.title: Step 1: Configure DNS
items.text: For the providers it knows, ./portcullis init (and later ./portcullis dns setup) creates every record below for you. For the others it prints them, and you create them by hand. See Record sets for the full list, CAA included.

items.title: Option A: Wildcard DNS Record (Recommended)
items.text:
Create a single wildcard A record pointing all subdomains to your server:

*.portcullis.example.com  A  203.0.113.10

This means auth.portcullis.example.com, hub.portcullis.example.com, grafana.portcullis.example.com, and every other service subdomain all resolve to your server without creating individual records.

You also need a record for the bare subdomain:

portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10

Cloudflare proxy

If using Cloudflare, disable the orange cloud (proxy) for the wildcard record. Cloudflare's proxy terminates TLS itself, so YubiKey and browser certificates never reach Portcullis. The DNS plan shows a proxied record as a wrong address and names it "proxied (orange cloud)".

items.title: Option B: Individual DNS Records
items.text:
If you prefer explicit records, create one for each service:

portcullis.example.com            A  203.0.113.10
auth.portcullis.example.com       A  203.0.113.10
directory.portcullis.example.com  A  203.0.113.10
enroll.portcullis.example.com     A  203.0.113.10
hub.portcullis.example.com        A  203.0.113.10
people.portcullis.example.com     A  203.0.113.10
traefik.portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10
metrics.portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10   (monitoring profile only)

You will need to add a record each time you enable a new app. dns setup only writes the wildcard pair (Option A); with Option B, dns plan shows the wildcard as missing.

items.title: Step 2: Create a DNS Provider API Token
items.text: Portcullis needs a DNS API token to solve ACME DNS-01 challenges for wildcard certificate issuance. Only *.portcullis.example.com appears in Certificate Transparency logs -- individual subdomain names are never leaked. The same token lets ./portcullis dns setup write the record sets.

items.title: Cloudflare
items.text:
1. Go to API Tokens
  2. Click "Create Token" and use the "Edit zone DNS" template
  3. Permissions: Zone > DNS > Edit. To let dns setup --dnssec turn on DNSSEC signing, also add Zone > DNS Settings > Edit
  4. Set in .env:
DNS_PROVIDER=cloudflare
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=your-token

items.title: Porkbun
items.text:
1. Go to API Access
  2. Enable API access for your domain
  3. Create an API key and secret key
  4. Set in .env:
DNS_PROVIDER=porkbun
PORKBUN_API_KEY=pk1_...
PORKBUN_SECRET_API_KEY=sk1_...

items.title: AWS Route 53
items.text:
DNS_PROVIDER=route53
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your-key
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your-secret
AWS_HOSTED_ZONE_ID=Z1234567890

AWS_HOSTED_ZONE_ID is optional: without it the zone is found with a SOA lookup. No AWS CLI is needed.

items.title: DigitalOcean
items.text:
DNS_PROVIDER=digitalocean
DO_AUTH_TOKEN=your-token

See DigitalOcean below for what Portcullis can and can't do there.

items.title: Hetzner
items.text:
Hetzner has two DNS APIs, so Portcullis has two providers:

# legacy DNS API (dns.hetzner.com)
DNS_PROVIDER=hetzner
HETZNER_API_KEY=your-key

# DNS in the Hetzner Cloud API (console.hetzner.com)
DNS_PROVIDER=hetzner-cloud
HETZNER_API_TOKEN=your-cloud-token

See Hetzner: legacy DNS and Hetzner Cloud for which one to pick.

items.title: Other lego providers
items.text: See Other providers: Traefik can still issue the certificate, but you create the records by hand.

items.title: First-time setup
items.text:
./portcullis init asks for your domain and DNS provider (credentials are read from the environment or a hidden prompt), writes them to .env and, for the providers it knows, creates the records from Step 1 for you (dns setup). At that point Traefik has no ACME account yet, so the CAA is the CA-only form (see CAA); the end of init pins it to Traefik's account once Traefik has registered:

./portcullis init

items.title: Creating or checking the records later
items.text:
./portcullis dns plan            # every record Portcullis wants vs what is live; changes nothing
./portcullis dns setup           # show the plan, confirm, write it through the provider API
./portcullis dns check           # public checks only (no credentials); exit 1 on a problem
  • dns plan prints one row per record (set, name, type, wanted, live, status), the steps left, the CAA judgement ("would issue: yes") and the DNSSEC state of the zone. With an automated provider it reads the provider's records too, and lists records under your domain that aren't Portcullis' (a CNAME to a name that doesn't exist, an address that isn't this server's, a leftover _acme-challenge TXT). --json prints the plan object (contract §12.2).
  • dns setup shows the plan and asks before it writes anything (--yes skips the question and is required without a terminal). It applies the address and caa sets (plus nomail with DNS_NOMAIL=true, or one set with --only address|caa|nomail), waits until the public resolvers show them stably (see CAA → TTLs and waits), then runs dns check. --dnssec also turns on DNSSEC signing (the question then says so: signing is zone-wide), see DNSSEC. With a provider it can't write to, it prints the records to create by hand and exits 0.
  • dns check asks only the public resolvers (1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8), so it needs no credentials. It exits 1 when a record or the DNSSEC state is a Problem.

The provider work runs in the domains image's one-shot tool (the dns-tool service): the credentials from .env reach it as JSON on its stdin, never on a command line, in a container's environment or in docker inspect, and its provider errors are redacted. See Security & Hardening and the CLI Reference.

./portcullis status has a DNS block for the main domain and every added domain: the addresses, the CAA pin, the DNSSEC state and records that aren't Portcullis'. It reads the domains service's plans, so it shows "DNS checks unavailable" while that service isn't running.

items.title: Changing the provider or credentials
items.text:
Edit .env:

ACME_EMAIL=admin@example.com
DNS_PROVIDER=porkbun
PORKBUN_API_KEY=pk1_...
PORKBUN_SECRET_API_KEY=sk1_...

Then restart the stack so Traefik picks up the new environment:

./portcullis up

Traefik requests and renews the wildcard certificate automatically. Run ./portcullis dns setup to write the records at the new provider.

Changing the domain

PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN is baked into the Keycloak realm (redirect URIs, hostname), LLDAP_BASE_DN, the server certificate and every enabled app's config. Pick it before init; changing it later means a new install.

items.title: Step 4: Verify
items.text:
Check that the certificate was issued:

# Check Traefik logs for ACME
docker compose logs traefik | grep -i acme

# Test with curl
curl -v https://auth.portcullis.example.com 2>&1 | grep "subject:"

You should see a Let's Encrypt certificate for *.portcullis.example.com.

Then check the records, the CAA pin and DNSSEC:

./portcullis dns check
dig +short CAA portcullis.example.com @1.1.1.1   # issue and issuewild, accounturi=… once Traefik has registered

items.title: Record sets
items.text:
A record set is the unit Portcullis owns: it writes, replaces and removes only the records of its sets, at three names: <d>, *.<d> and _dmarc.<d>. It never touches NS, SOA, the apex of a zone it doesn't own (example.com when <d> is portcullis.example.com) or any other record, except under the CAA merge rule.

Set Records TTL Default address <d> and *.<d>: A → the server's IPv4, AAAA → its IPv6 (no AAAA without one) 300 on caa at <d> only (it also covers *.<d>): issue and issuewild for the ACME CA, optional iodef 300 on (DNS_CAA=true), when the CA is known nomail at <d>: null MX 0 . and TXT v=spf1 -all; at _dmarc.<d>: TXT v=DMARC1; p=reject; 3600 off
  • address is refused while a CNAME exists at <d> or *.<d>: the plan shows the CNAME as a record that isn't Portcullis' and names it, and you remove it by hand.
  • nomail says "this domain sends no mail", so nobody can send mail that passes as yours. Turn it on for the main domain with DNS_NOMAIL=true (then dns setup); for an added domain, use its Fix in the Hub's DNS panel. The plan recommends it (Info) when <d> has no MX and no SPF record and ALERT_SMTP_FROM isn't at or under <d>. It replaces an existing SPF, MX or DMARC record at those names, and the plan says so first. Other TXT records at <d> (site verifications) stay.

items.title: CAA
items.text:
A CAA record says which certificate authorities may issue certificates for a name. Portcullis' CAA allows only the ACME CA in use, only its own ACME account, and only by DNS-01, so nobody else (another CA, another Let's Encrypt account, an HTTP-01 challenge) can get a certificate for your names:

portcullis.example.com  CAA  0 issue "letsencrypt.org; accounturi=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/123; validationmethods=dns-01"
portcullis.example.com  CAA  0 issuewild "letsencrypt.org; accounturi=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/123; validationmethods=dns-01"

issuewild is written explicitly because every Portcullis certificate is a wildcard. With DNS_CAA_IODEF set (e.g. mailto:security@example.com) a 0 iodef "<DNS_CAA_IODEF>" entry is added: where CAs may report refused orders (few act on it).

Pin vs CA-only. The pin names the account (accounturi=). While no account is known yet, Portcullis writes the CA-only form, which still allows only one CA and only DNS-01:

portcullis.example.com  CAA  0 issue "letsencrypt.org; validationmethods=dns-01"
portcullis.example.com  CAA  0 issuewild "letsencrypt.org; validationmethods=dns-01"

Which account. The main domain is pinned to Traefik's ACME account (./portcullis reads only its URI from Traefik's acme.json, which never leaves its volume). Each added domain is pinned to the domains service's account. So the domains service can't get a certificate for the main domain, and Traefik can't for an added domain. An added subdomain of the main domain (team-a.<d>) gets its own CAA at its name: the closest CAA wins, so the main domain's pin neither blocks it nor gets widened.

Merge rule. At a name that already has CAA records, Portcullis replaces only the entries for its CA (matched case-insensitively, ignoring a trailing dot and spaces); iodef only when DNS_CAA_IODEF is set. Other CAs' entries stay, and the plan shows an Info "other CAs may also issue for : digicert.com". Writing issuewild takes wildcard issuance away from another CA that had only issue, and the plan says so. On an added zone apex the plan notes that the CAA covers every name in the zone without CAA of its own.

Would issue. The plan judges the live CAA the way the CA does: it finds the closest CAA set for <d> and for *.<d> (climbing the labels), at both public resolvers, and asks whether that set allows the CA, the account and DNS-01. A failed lookup or a critical entry it doesn't know counts as no.

Account switches. CAA isn't checked when an account registers, only when it orders, so the order of steps matters:

  • Added domains. The domains service registers a new account (the first time, or when ACME_CA_SERVER or ACME_EMAIL changed), writes the new pin to every added domain, waits until both public resolvers see it, and only then orders. There is never a gap.
  • Main domain. Traefik registers and orders in one go, so ./portcullis works around it. The CAA is CA-only while Traefik has no account. ./portcullis up and upgrade read Traefik's account URI once its resolver is running (waiting up to 3 minutes for a first registration), record it in secrets/domains/main-domain.env, and tighten the pin when the live one differs. A failure there only warns, and a pin that was written but isn't visible everywhere yet says so ("was written, but it is not visible yet at 8.8.8.8: those caches clear within …"), never "could not pin". ./portcullis config apply on an ACME_STAGING flip relaxes the CAA to CA-only with Traefik still running, waits until no cache can still hold the old pin (saving that point, so a rerun waits for it too), and only then stops Traefik, clears acme.json and starts it again; if the relax fails or hasn't settled it stops there, fail safe (see Certificates → Switching).

  • Changes made elsewhere. ./portcullis status has the main domain's plan rebuilt for it (at most once per 30 s), so a CAA changed at the provider shows at once; when the rebuild fails it says the lines may be stale.

  • Lost account. When Traefik's acme.json is gone (the volume deleted or recreated), Traefik registers a new account by itself, and its renewal then fails on CAA. ./portcullis status shows the Problem "CAA allows another ACME account than Traefik's — fix: ./portcullis dns setup" when secrets/domains/main-domain.env names a different account than Traefik's current one. A missing main-domain.env (Traefik hadn't registered yet when up ran) is only a Warning; dns plan, dns setup and dns check write it as soon as they read Traefik's account. Backup and restore keep both accounts, so a restore doesn't cause this.

TTLs and waits. Portcullis asks for TTL 300 for the caa set, but a provider may store more: Porkbun raises every TTL under 600 s to 600. Resolvers then keep the old CAA for up to 10 minutes. So every wait after a write (dns setup, the tighten after up, the relax on a flip) follows the TTL caches got, read before and after the write: the TTL the provider stores (a stored 0 or 1 — Cloudflare's "auto", Hetzner's zone default — counts as unknown) or the one the zone's authoritative nameservers serve, whichever is longer: up to that TTL + 1 minute, longer while a resolver's answer shows it keeps its copy longer (its remaining TTL; for a record that didn't exist, the zone's negative-caching TTL from its SOA), at most 15 minutes. A public resolver is a pool of many caches (anycast): one round where it shows the new records doesn't mean the next answer will, so a wait counts the records as visible only when both resolvers showed them in 4 rounds in a row (10 s apart, at least 30 s), and every remaining TTL a resolver reported for an old CAA answer has run out (Google Public DNS has been seen re-serving an old pin with an almost fresh TTL minutes after the change). So ./portcullis status right after dns setup normally shows the CAA as planned. The tighten after up / upgrade / init isn't a safety step, so it waits for stable answers at most 3 minutes, then goes on with a "written; not yet stable at " warning: status, which builds a fresh plan each run, may show the CAA as not yet as planned until those caches have cleared (the time the warning gives); the Hub's DNS panel shows its cached plan, rebuilt within 5 minutes. dns setup keeps the 15-minute bound, and the relax on a flip is never shortened. The relax on a flip also waits out the TTL itself, since the CA's resolvers can't be asked. When a wait hits its bound, the records were written: the warning says "written; not yet stable at ", how long it may still serve the old records and until when (every time Portcullis prints is rounded up to the minute and dated: 2026-11-14 07:19 UTC), and ./portcullis status shows the CAA as planned once that has passed. A write that failed is a separate message.

Settings (.env):

Variable Default Meaning DNS_CAA true Write the caa set (true or false only: anything else fails, so a typo can't switch CAA off). false removes the entries Portcullis wrote: for an added domain exactly those it tracked; for the main domain (dns setup) the entries for its CA that carry validationmethods=dns-01. Your own entries for the same CA without that parameter stay DNS_CAA_ISSUER empty The CAA identifier of a CA other than Let's Encrypt. Let's Encrypt production and staging are both letsencrypt.org. Any other ACME_CA_SERVER without it: no caa set, and an Info "CAA skipped: unknown CA" DNS_CAA_IODEF empty The iodef target (mailto: or https:); empty: no iodef entry DNS_NOMAIL false Add the nomail set to the main domain (dns setup)

After changing them, run ./portcullis up (the domains service reads them) and ./portcullis dns setup.

Providers without automation. With a lego-only provider, dns plan prints the exact CAA records to add by hand: CA-only before Traefik has registered, pinned after. dns check and status check them. up doesn't tighten them and config apply can't relax them for you: change them by hand before an ACME_STAGING flip (to CA-only) and after (to the new pin that dns plan shows).

items.title: DNSSEC
items.text:
DNSSEC signs a zone's records, so validating resolvers can tell forged answers from real ones. It needs two things: the zone signed at your DNS provider, and a DS record (a digest of the zone's signing key) published at the parent zone, which you do at your registrar. Portcullis checks the chain for every name, at both public resolvers, and shows one state with the step that is left:

State Meaning Severity What to do secure The DS matches the zone's key and both resolvers validate ok Nothing unsigned No signing key, no DS Info Turn on signing at the provider (Cloudflare: ./portcullis dns setup --dnssec, or one click in the Hub for an added domain), then publish the DS ds_missing Signed, but no DS at the parent Warning Add the DS the plan shows (key tag, algorithm, digest type 2, digest) at your registrar ds_mismatch / bogus A DS that matches no key, or validation fails Problem Validating resolvers can't reach the domain. Fix the DS at the registrar to the values the plan shows, or remove the DS insecure Signed and the DS matches, but the resolvers don't validate the parent zone above it Info Nothing in this zone: the chain above it isn't signed or validated unknown The lookups failed Warning Retry; the plan shows the resolver error

Never turn signing off while a DS record is published

Never turn signing off while a DS record is published: validating resolvers then can't reach the domain. To stop using DNSSEC, remove the DS at the registrar first, wait for its TTL to expire, then turn signing off at the provider. Portcullis never turns signing off and never removes a DS.

Turning signing on is opt-in and never automatic, because it is zone-wide: it also affects your other names in the zone (for portcullis.example.com, all of example.com).

  • Main domain: ./portcullis dns setup --dnssec (Cloudflare only; with other providers it prints the steps).
  • Added domain: Turn on DNSSEC signing in the Hub's DNS panel, or the doctor's one-click fix, both behind a confirmation naming the zone.
  • Through its API only Cloudflare can sign. A 403 means the token lacks Zone > DNS Settings > Edit. Route 53 signing needs a KMS key and stays manual (the plan reads the DS values when the IAM policy allows GetDNSSEC). Porkbun's API doesn't sign zones. DigitalOcean has no DNSSEC.

Publishing the DS at the registrar. Once the zone is signed, dns plan (or the Hub's DNS panel, with a Copy button per value) shows the DS:

DS: key tag 2371, algorithm 13, digest type 2, digest 1F98…

At the registrar, open the domain's DNSSEC (or "DS records") settings, add a record with exactly these four values, and save. With Cloudflare as registrar Cloudflare publishes it by itself. The state moves from ds_missing to secure once the parent zone serves the DS (minutes to a few hours, depending on the registry).

items.title: Hetzner: legacy DNS and Hetzner Cloud
items.text:
Hetzner moved DNS into the Hetzner Cloud API, and new zones can't be created on the legacy dns.hetzner.com any more. Pick the provider by where the zone lives:

Provider Zone at .env credential Hub field hetzner the legacy DNS console (dns.hetzner.com) HETZNER_API_KEY DNS API token (legacy dns.hetzner.com) hetzner-cloud a Hetzner Cloud project (console.hetzner.com) HETZNER_API_TOKEN (a Cloud API token with Read & Write) Hetzner Cloud API token (Read & Write)

The main domain's certificate works with both: Traefik's lego provider hetzner uses the Cloud API when HETZNER_API_TOKEN is set, and the legacy API with HETZNER_API_KEY. config apply (which up runs too) maps hetzner-cloud to it, so set only the one variable that matches DNS_PROVIDER: it refuses hetzner with HETZNER_API_TOKEN set (lego would use the Cloud API) and hetzner-cloud with HETZNER_API_KEY set. Neither API signs zones through Portcullis; the plan shows the DNSSEC steps.

items.title: DigitalOcean
items.text:
Portcullis writes DigitalOcean records through DigitalOcean's own API client, so CAA records get their flags and tag. DigitalOcean has no DNSSEC: the plan's step for an unsigned zone is "digitalocean can't sign: move the zone to sign it".

Portcullis' DigitalOcean support is tested only against a stand-in for DigitalOcean's API, not yet on a real account. In particular, whether DigitalOcean accepts the null MX 0 . of the nomail set, and stores CAA flags and tags exactly as written, is unverified. After dns setup (or a Fix in the Hub), run ./portcullis dns check and look at the caa and nomail rows. If DigitalOcean refuses a record, the tool exits with the provider's (redacted) error.

items.title: Other providers
items.text:
Traefik supports 80+ DNS providers via lego. Set DNS_PROVIDER=<lego-provider-name> and its required environment variables in .env. Traefik then issues the certificate, but ./portcullis can't write records there: init and dns setup print the records of the record sets to create by hand, CAA included (see Providers without automation). dns check and status check them all the same. Added domains in the Hub need one of the automated providers.

Traefik is configured entirely through environment variables in the core docker-compose.yml (there is no traefik.yml). If your provider's environment variables are not already listed there, add them to the traefik service's environment section in a docker-compose.override.yml (it is part of every backup).

items.title: How ACME DNS-01 Works
items.text:
Unlike HTTP-01 challenges (which require port 80 access for each hostname), DNS-01 proves domain ownership by creating a TXT record in your DNS zone:

  1. Traefik requests a wildcard certificate for *.portcullis.example.com
  2. Let's Encrypt responds with a challenge token
  3. Traefik uses your DNS provider's API to create a _acme-challenge.portcullis.example.com TXT record
  4. Let's Encrypt verifies the TXT record exists
  5. The wildcard certificate is issued, covering all subdomains

This is why Portcullis needs your DNS provider API token -- it creates and cleans up the challenge TXT record automatically.

items.title: One domain per installation
items.text:
A Portcullis installation serves exactly one base domain, PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN, and every app lives at <subdomain>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}. This is enforced, not just a default:

  • group-gate denies every request whose host is not exactly <label>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}, because it looks policies and groups up by that label
  • the Hub rejects templates whose routers use any other domain (Integration Contracts §4)
  • Traefik requests one wildcard certificate (${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN} and *.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN})
  • oauth2-proxy's cookie and redirect whitelist cover .${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN} only
  • Keycloak's hostname is auth.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}

To serve a second domain, run a second installation. Supporting several domains in one installation would need all of the following:

  • group-gate keyed by full host, or by a domain list
  • the Hub's host validation and policy file keyed the same way
  • a certificate and DNS records per domain
  • oauth2-proxy cookies per domain: a session cookie can't span unrelated domains, so users would sign in once per domain
  • Keycloak redirect URIs for each domain

items.title: Local Development (No Public Domain)
items.text:
For local development without a real domain or ACME:

  1. Run ./portcullis init --domain portcullis.local --dns-provider none. init already issues a self-signed *.portcullis.local server certificate from the internal PKI (certs/server.crt; ./portcullis pki setup --with-server-cert recreates it)
  2. Add entries to /etc/hosts:
127.0.0.1  portcullis.local auth.portcullis.local directory.portcullis.local enroll.portcullis.local hub.portcullis.local people.portcullis.local traefik.portcullis.local
  1. Import certs/root-ca.crt into your browser or OS trust store to avoid certificate warnings

Note

YubiKey and browser certificates work the same way locally. The only difference is the website certificate (HTTPS) is self-signed instead of from Let's Encrypt.

items.title: Adding extra domains
items.text:
Beyond the main domain, Portcullis can serve extra domains with their own wildcard website certificates (HTTPS). Extra domains are added in the Hub's Settings → Domains section with + Add domain (see Hub Management).

Each added domain:

  • has its own A/AAAA records (<d> and *.<d>) managed by the domains service
  • gets its own CAA, pinned to the domains service's ACME account (see CAA)
  • gets its own Let's Encrypt wildcard certificate via DNS-01
  • can host app instances with hostnames on that domain
  • has a DNS panel in the Hub with its plan, a Fix button per record set and its DNSSEC state (see Hub Management)

Supported providers: Cloudflare, Porkbun, Route 53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner (legacy DNS) and Hetzner Cloud (the same list as the main domain's dns setup, minus none).

Server addresses. The records point at the server's public IPv4 (and IPv6), from PORTCULLIS_PUBLIC_IPV4 / _IPV6 in .env or detected by ./portcullis up (see Security & Hardening).

Added subdomains of the main domain (e.g. team-a.<main domain>) are allowed. This lets you delegate zones of your main domain to Portcullis without changing the main domain's DNS setup. The added subdomain gets its own wildcard certificate, and app instances on it use the cross-domain sign-in flow (see Hub Management).

Core services stay on the main domain: the portal, Hub, people, auth, directory, enroll (setup links), traefik, metrics and mcp endpoints are never served on extra domains (an app's own MCP endpoint is on the app's host, wherever it is).

Removing an added domain is allowed only when no app instance has a hostname on it. The domains service removes the DNS records it created, its CAA entries included (only the exact values it wrote; other CAs' entries and your own records stay, also on Porkbun and the legacy Hetzner API, where it deletes each record by its ID), and retries once on failure.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text: Get Portcullis running from zero to a working authentication gateway with one command: ./portcullis init.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Docker with the compose plugin, v2.24.4 or later (env_file with required: false, the Hub's !override labels) -- Install Docker To run everything as one unprivileged account instead, use rootless Podman 5.4 or later with the Docker CLI and compose plugin: see Rootless Podman.
  • openssl, jq and curl on the host (the CLI checks for them)
  • A domain you control, with DNS hosted at a provider Traefik's ACME client (lego) supports: Cloudflare, Porkbun, Route53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, ... (see DNS Configuration)
  • A server with ports 80 and 443 reachable (VPS, home server, or local machine)
  • A YubiKey (or another FIDO2 key) for WebAuthn. ykman is only needed for YubiKey certificates (PIV)

items.title: Before you start: DNS
items.text:
Portcullis gets one Let's Encrypt wildcard certificate for *.<domain> with an ACME DNS-01 challenge. Without working DNS, Traefik can't get a certificate and every page shows a browser warning. Two things must be in place:

  1. The domain's DNS is hosted at a supported provider, and you have an API token that can edit its DNS records. Traefik uses the token to create the temporary _acme-challenge TXT record. The token is needed even if you create the A/AAAA records yourself. Per-provider steps (Cloudflare: "Edit zone DNS", Porkbun, Route 53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, others) are in DNS Configuration → Step 2.
  2. Records pointing at the server: <domain> and *.<domain> (A, and AAAA if the host has IPv6) → the server's public IP. ./portcullis init creates them for the providers it knows (dns setup), or prints them for you to create by hand. See DNS Configuration → Step 1.

Check before running init (or right after, if it created the records):

dig +short portcullis.example.com
dig +short test.portcullis.example.com   # any name: answered by the wildcard

Both must return the server's public IP. ./portcullis dns check checks the same and more. CAA is handled by dns setup: it writes a CAA that allows only Let's Encrypt, only by DNS-01 and, once Traefik has registered, only Traefik's ACME account. CAA entries of other CAs already at the name stay (DNS Configuration → CAA).

Tip

For a first try, set ACME_STAGING=true in .env (see the table below): Let's Encrypt's staging service has no rate limits, so DNS mistakes don't lock you out for an hour. Switch it off with ./portcullis config apply once everything works.

No public domain (local testing)? Use --dns-provider none and the self-signed setup in DNS Configuration → Local Development.

items.title: Step 1: Clone the core repository
items.text:
git clone git@github.com:porelli/portcullis.git
cd portcullis

That is all you need to clone. The Hub image is pulled from ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub and the Keycloak image (Keycloak with Portcullis's sign-in extension) from ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-keycloak (no build step), and the Hub clones the app templates from porelli/portcullis-templates on first start.

items.title: Step 2: Run portcullis init
items.text:
./portcullis init

It prompts for:

  • Domain: your base domain, e.g. portcullis.example.com. Apps live at <name>.<domain>
  • Email for Let's Encrypt notices (default admin@<domain>)
  • DNS provider (default cloudflare) and its API credentials, read with a hidden prompt

Unattended:

CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... ./portcullis init --non-interactive \
  --domain portcullis.example.com --dns-provider cloudflare

All options are in the CLI Reference.

items.title: What init does
items.text:
1. Writes .env (mode 0600) with every secret randomly generated: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD, LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, LLDAP_JWT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET, HUB_PROXY_SECRET, and BACKUP_PASSWORD (encrypts off-host backups). Docker compose refuses to start if any of them is missing, so there are no default passwords. An existing .env is kept; only empty or missing secrets are filled in.
  2. Creates DNS records for <domain> and *.<domain> pointing at this host's public IP, and the CA-only CAA (dns setup; skipped with --skip-dns or --dns-provider none). Its last step pins the CAA to Traefik's ACME account once Traefik has registered. The wildcard covers all app and core subdomains: auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, people, metrics, mcp (the "All my apps" MCP endpoint, AI support), and each enabled app.
  3. Initialises Vault in server mode with persistent raft storage. The root token and unseal key go to secrets/ (see the warning below), and the enroll service gets a least-privilege AppRole. Vault unseals itself on every start from then on.
  4. Starts the core stack (docker compose up -d --build) and waits for Vault, PostgreSQL, LLDAP and Keycloak to be healthy.
  5. Creates the internal certificate authority in Vault: the root and two intermediate CAs, for YubiKey certificates and browser certificates, Keycloak's truststore, and a self-signed wildcard server cert for local use.
  6. Configures Keycloak: imports the portcullis realm (passkeys, YubiKey and browser certificates, LLDAP federation, step-up flows) and registers the forward-auth OIDC client with the secret from .env.
  7. Creates config/, a separate git repo holding your .env and overrides (skip with --no-config-repo; see CLI Reference).
  8. Prints the URLs of the core pages (directory, identity provider, Hub, Traefik dashboard).

Every step is idempotent: if something fails (DNS not propagated yet, a slow image pull), fix it and run ./portcullis init again.

Back up secrets/ now, offline

secrets/vault-init.json holds the Vault root token and the unseal key. Losing it together with the host means losing the CA, and every YubiKey and browser certificate with it. Anyone who has it can unseal Vault. Keep an offline copy, and treat backups made by ./portcullis backup the same way: they contain secrets/ and .env. Store BACKUP_PASSWORD offline too: without it, off-host backups can't be restored after losing the host (see Backups).

items.title: Settings in .env worth knowing
items.text:
init writes sensible defaults. The full reference with comments is .env.example in the core repo.

Variable Default Notes ACME_STAGING false true uses Let's Encrypt staging (untrusted certs, no rate limits). Apply with ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up CLIENT_CERT_TTL 720h Longest lifetime of a YubiKey or browser certificate (30 days) HUB_PROXY_SECRET generated Shared secret Traefik adds to every request to the Hub. The Hub refuses to start without it (at least 32 characters) HUB_IMAGE ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:edge on core main Hub image. edge is the latest build of the Hub's main; a core release pins a released tag by digest. If you override it, use a released tag with its digest, e.g. ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3@sha256:… (see Upgrading & Releases) KEYCLOAK_IMAGE ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-keycloak:edge on core main Keycloak image (the official Keycloak plus the sign-in extension). Same rules as HUB_IMAGE: edge is the latest build of its main; pin a released tag with its digest if you override it BACKUP_PASSWORD generated restic repository password for ./portcullis backup --offsite. Keep an offline copy; never rotate it BACKUP_REPOSITORY unset restic repository for off-host backups (s3:, b2:, rest:, …). See Backups COMPOSE_PROFILES unset monitoring enables Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana at metrics.<domain>. See Monitoring HUB_SHARED_ENV empty Extra variable names the Hub may pass to templates. Core secrets are refused HUB_OVERRIDE_BIND_ROOTS /srv:/mnt:/media Host directories an app's custom compose override (Hub → Expert) may bind-mount. System paths and / are refused PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET 172.31.250.0/24 Fixed subnet of the shared portcullis-proxy network PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE 172.31.250.128/25 Dynamic addresses for app containers. Must be inside the subnet and must not contain Traefik's IP PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP 172.31.250.2 Traefik's static IP on portcullis-proxy. Header-auth apps trust identity headers only from this address PORTCULLIS_AUTH_SUBNET 172.31.251.0/28 Internal Traefik ↔ Keycloak network portcullis-auth. Must not overlap the proxy subnet PORTCULLIS_AUTH_IP_RANGE 172.31.251.8/29 Dynamic range on portcullis-auth PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP 172.31.251.2 The only address Keycloak accepts proxy headers (incl. the forwarded YubiKey or browser certificate) from HUB_PEOPLE_ADDR :8889 Hub's people listener port (set by core, not operator config). Accessible to any signed-in user at people.<domain>

Change the network ranges before init, not after

Only change the PORTCULLIS_*_SUBNET / _IP_RANGE / _TRAEFIK_IP values if they collide with a host, LAN or VPN network, and do it before the first init (./portcullis init --env-only writes .env and stops, so you can edit it). Docker cannot change an existing network. For portcullis-proxy you would have to disable the apps in the Hub, run ./portcullis down, docker network rm portcullis-proxy, ./portcullis up, and re-enable the apps. ./portcullis up detects the mismatch and prints these steps. See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Step 3: Wait for the certificate
items.text:
Traefik requests the wildcard certificate with an ACME DNS-01 challenge. This usually takes 1-3 minutes:

docker compose logs -f traefik 2>&1 | grep -i acme
./portcullis status        # overall health; exits 1 if something is down

No certificate after a few minutes? Check, in this order:

  • ./portcullis dns check (are the records right and public, would the CA issue?);
  • the provider token: it must be allowed to edit DNS records of this zone (a read-only or wrong-zone token fails the challenge);
  • the Traefik log for acme errors such as rateLimited (use ACME_STAGING=true while testing) or CAA (./portcullis dns setup pins the CAA to Traefik's current account);
  • to change the provider or token, follow DNS Configuration → Changing the provider or credentials.

items.title: Step 4: First sign-in (setup link)
items.text:
The admin account never signs in with a password (and the password method starts switched off for everyone, see Sign-in Methods). ./portcullis init ends with a one-time setup link for the LLDAP admin:

  1. Open the link, click Register my key and touch your YubiKey (set or enter its PIN).
  2. You are signed in and land in the Hub. No LLDAP or Keycloak login.
  3. Every later sign-in is Sign in with Passkey and one touch.

The link works once and expires after 72 h. A new one only from the server: ./portcullis invite admin --to hub adds another key (a spare); ./portcullis invite admin --to hub --replace-keys is for a lost or stolen key (removes the old keys first). The Hub never issues links for administrators.

items.title: Step 5: Create users
items.text:
In the Hub, Users & Groups (or LLDAP at https://directory.<your-domain>, which keeps its own admin / LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD login):

  1. Create the user. The username is the user's identity everywhere (it can't be changed later). The email is only profile data: users can edit it themselves, so it is never used to identify or link accounts.
  2. Add the user to the groups of the apps they need, e.g. users_grafana. Members of lldap_admin can reach the core admin UIs (Hub, directory, Traefik dashboard, Keycloak's realm console).
  3. Send the user their setup link (the Hub shows it once; on the server: ./portcullis invite <user>). It lands them on https://<your-domain>/, the portal with the apps they may use.

Keycloak reads users and groups from LLDAP through its LDAP federation.

items.title: Step 6: Enable your first app
items.text:
In the Hub:

  1. Browse the Marketplace and open an app (e.g. Grafana).
  2. Fill in any required settings (media paths, etc.).
  3. Click Enable. The Hub starts the app as its own compose project, registers its Keycloak client if it has one, and publishes its group and policy to group-gate.

The app is reachable at its subdomain. Users need the app's users_<app> group if the app enforces group access.

items.title: Step 7 (optional): YubiKey and browser certificates
items.text:
For YubiKey certificates (PIV), an admin issues one on the host with the YubiKey attached:

./portcullis cert enroll alice alice@example.com

or pastes a CSR made with ykman on the person's Sign-in tab on https://people.<your-domain>/. Certificates last 30 days. People renew their own on their Sign-in page, https://people.<your-domain>/signin.

Browser certificates start off: switch Browser certificate on in Hub → Settings → Sign-in, and people can create one (a .p12 file) on their Sign-in page. See Certificates and Sign-in methods.

items.title: Day-to-day
items.text:
./portcullis status                # health
./portcullis up / down             # start / stop the core stack
git pull && ./portcullis upgrade   # update (backs up first)
./portcullis backup --offsite      # backup, also to restic (schedule it: backup schedule --systemd)
./portcullis version               # core version + Hub and Keycloak images
